, neural modeling remains a complex endeavor. While a comprehensive and accessible online collection of neural system models is currently absent, the NEURON simulator offers an open-source library of both historical and contemporary models. However, these collections lack interactive three-dimensional representations, which hinders a deeper intuitive understanding. This paper presents an open-source, web-based application designed for the interactive visualization of NEURON models. We demonstrate the utility of this tool through the examination of a classic neurobiology experiment: the propagation of an action potential along a myelinated axon. While existing literature typically focuses on axons as one-dimensional lines, our application allows for the investigation of action potential dynamics along the axial, vertical, and lateral dimensions of a three-dimensional axon. The proposed platform serves as a valuable resource for visualizing neural models, fostering an increased intuitive grasp of neurobiology. Its capacity to enhance the visualization of scientific phenomena positions it as a significant asset for both scientific communication and education. The application is publicly accessible at https://neuron-visualizer.org, and the source code can be found at https://github.com/NeuronVisualizer. Additionally, the code has been integrated into the NEURON release version 8.0.4 via the accompanying source repository. Our findings indicate that the NEURON visualizer effectively improves intuition regarding action potential propagation within a realistic three-dimensional axon, a capability that current visual representations fail to support. Furthermore, the NEURON visualizer enables users to investigate the similarities, differences, and underlying mechanisms of various action potentials across multiple axons. We demonstrate this functionality using two integrated-circuit models and a squid giant axon, showcasing how the NEURON visualizer promotes a more intuitive comprehension of the biophysics governing axon physiology. We demonstrate the potential of the NEURON visualizer to improve both informal and formal neural biology education by highlighting its current capabilities and future capabilities. Specifically, we illustrate how the tool can enhance undergraduate laboratory sessions, emphasizing the advantages of incorporating three-dimensional visualizations of axons and their associated physiological phenomena. Additionally, the NEURON visualizer is fully compatible with the curriculum outlined in Wilson et al. (2019), which is widely adopted in undergraduate institutions. Finally, we show that the NEURON visualizer enhances the visualization of complex neuroscience concepts, such as axon branching, and its source code has already been incorporated into the NEURON release 8.0.4. The NEURON visualizer receives active community support and actively seeks user contributions

restrict the physical characteristics of planets in compact systems. The multi-period light curve of HD 80606 b records 32 years of data, spanning over 10 million days. By analyzing the interval between consecutive transit midpoints at a daily resolution, we identified 7,254 anomalous values. Statistical analysis revealed that these outliers cluster exclusively around the transit period, exhibiting both positive and negative shifts, with the positive deviations showing a strong correlation to the total system brightness. This behavior is best explained by dust clouds resulting from meteoritic activity. After removing these outliers, we re-evaluates the period anomalies to find additional candidates linked to other phenomena. We discovered that most remaining anomalies occur either shortly before or long after the transit transit, with a notable group appearing more than 100 days post-transit. Furthermore, these anomalies are not randomly distributed; they show a dependence on the system brightness during the preceding transit, a relationship best accounted for by orbital scattering caused by close approach perturbations from a perturbing body. Finally, we employs the Detrended Cross-correlation Coefficient (DCCC) to quantify the long-term periodicity of these post-transit anomalies, demonstrating that they are correlated with the transit-inclination angle on a timescale matching the orbital period of the perturber, which is estimated to be between 200 and 350 days. This period aligns with reported 200–300 day orbital periods, suggesting that 86% of the post-transit-DCCC anomalies stem from orbital scattering induced by a body with this orbital cycle. These findings underscore the value of extended light curve observations in elucidating orbital dynamics in compact systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the detected post-transit anomalies serve as a diagnostic tool for scattering events, enabling estimation of the orbital period of the responsible body without the need to model light curves from non-transiting planets. Ultimately, this methodology paves the way for constraining orbital periods of non-transiting planets and distinguishing their signatures from those of meteoritic activity. Graphene and graphitic liquid capillaries have emerged as a promising method for transferring mass and energy in micro- and nanosystems. To date, research has primarily focused on capillary effects in single- and few-layer graphene. In contrast, the phenomena occurring at the atomic scale within graphitic liquid films remain poorly understood. This study reports the observed atomic structures of liquid films in graphite at room temperature, contrasting them with those in graphene-based liquid capillaries and comparing them to conventional liquids. Unlike the former, the latter exhibit no distinct atomic structures. Based on these observations and their underlying physical mechanisms, we propose a theoretical model for the atomic structures of liquid films in graphite. These insights may aid in the rational design of graphene atomic capillaries. (Paper Scipdf URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.11771) [22 pages, 11 figures, 1 table, 138KB, 2022-02-12]

However, many of the queries researchers typically need to address—such as identifying proofs validated by specific versions of Isabelle/HOL or determining when a proof relied on a withdrawn theory—cannot be answered directly from the archive. This paper presents an initial attempt to construct a searchable, queryable version of the Isabelle Archive suitable for such analysis. We demonstrate the search for a specific state-of-the-art survey on theories dependent on high-level object logics, illustrating how the resulting statistics can guide future work. The resulting tool, developed in Python, performs the search directly against the raw ISO format stored in the archive; the accompanying code and a live demo are available online. Furthermore, we outline potential future enhancements, including indexing the theory documents within the archive. All findings and resources are also publicly accessible through an article in the Isabelle/HPF'21 proceedings. to identify interplanetary scalar and vector magnetic field wavelets (BWls), a method now considered a standard technique for characterizing solar origin waves. This study examines and compares the consistency among four distinct BWl classification schemes introduced over the past forty years: Hones (1970), Schwartz (1972), a combination of Schwartz (1972) and Heiles (1973), and a novel scheme also integrating Heiles' (1973) work. The analysis focuses on BWls recorded during 2014 at one-hour resolution near 1 AU using in situ data from the Advanced Composition Explorer (ACE). These BWls were randomly selected from 365 instances representing each of the twelve categories defined by the integration of all four classification schemes. Findings indicate that BWls with distinct morphologies can fall into the same category under different schemes, and that the frequency distribution of these schemes varies significantly across the population of solar magnetic BWls observed at 1 AU. Specifically, Scheme A, which combines Heones with the Schwartz-Heiles subset, tends to yield larger BWls. Consequently, the selection of a BWl scheme is intrins linked to scientific goals, such as determining the optimal method for correlating spacecraft observations with in-situ magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations. Finally, these four schemes are publicly released and accessible via a Python package, which is available on GitHub. This package is demonstrated to classify a sample of BWls from a time series of simulated interplanetary magnetic fields at 1 AU, as previously published in Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics (2019). The results confirm that the package's performance is comparable to that of the true data analysis, suggesting that Scheme A is well-suited for the comparison studies it facilitates. As a supplementary technique to the MHD simulation, it can help enhance the robustness of BWl studies. In this context, the package serves as an open-source resource that complements existing literature. Keywords: Wavelets; Magnetic fields.

in information fusion have become a focal point. Multi-valued-valued neural networks (MVVNs) have garnered significant attention as a mathematical foundation for information fusion. Among various multi-valued boolean functions, majority multi-valued valuations are particularly notable due to their simplicity and symmetry. Numerous multi-valued valuations are employed to encode different characteristics of high-order multi-valued functions. Leveraging concepts from multi-valued logic, this paper presents two intelligent multi-valued valuations, HM2 and SM2. These valuations are fully adaptive, meaning the threshold for aggregating inputs is determined by the input data itself. We demonstrate that the value outputs of valuations HM2 and SM2 can model the membership and negation of fuzzy sets, respectively. Additionally, both valuations can simulate any multi-valued valuation. We constructed two multi-valued aggregation functions based on HM2 and SM2, offering two distinct methods for high-order multi-valued aggregation. Both functions retain the properties of inputs, return values within the set {0, 1, 2}, and maintain monotonicity. Furthermore, we propose data fusion schemes utilizing these fully adaptive mechanisms. Ultimately, HM2 and SM2 offer two distinct approaches for data aggregation within multi-valued contexts. To validate the effectiveness of these fully adaptive mechanisms, we conducted benchmarking and comparative analyses, the results of which are detailed at the end of this paper. To our knowledge, this represents one of the earliest applications of fully adaptive multi-valued aggregation functions in data aggregation. Future work will explore the specific needs of various data types, such as fuzzy or probabilistic data, to identify the most appropriate fully adaptive multi-valued aggregation function for specific data characteristics. This paper demonstrates that a group-theoretic near exponential sequence cannot be approximated by a true exponential sequence. Furthermore, we establish that the Walnut near exponential sequence for natural numbers lacks a group-theoretic near exponential sequence within integers. Consequently, we conclude that a group-theoretic near exponential sequence and its corresponding natural number extension must differ. As a direct consequence, we prove that the Walnut near exponential sequence for natural numbers is not a group-theoretic near exponential sequence. Therefore, established theorems regarding genuine near power functions of exponent 2 in $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}$, or $\mathbb{R}$ are inapplicable to these sequences. Finally, we demonstrate that the Walsh near exponential sequence is not a group-theoretic near exponential sequence. Collectively, these findings indicate that group-theoretic near exponential sequences are significantly more complex than true exponential sequences. Furthermore, these results imply that existing theorems concerning near power functions of exponent 2 for group-theoretic near exponential sequences in $\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{R}$ are insufficient to characterize their behavior. This underscores the distinct nature of group-theoretic near exponential sequences and highlights the necessity of developing novel theories to analyze them. Such an approach could yield deeper insights into the arithmetic properties of these sequences and facilitate their practical application. At the conclusion of this paper, we propose potential future research directions, beginning with characterizing group-theoretic near exponential sequences in $\mathbb{Z}$. Additionally, we illustrate how functions related to the M\"obius inversion formula serve as compelling candidates for group-theoretic near exponential sequences, as they typically fall between two different orderings of near power functions. Characterizing these sequences could significantly advance the theory of near exponential sequences. This could, in turn, enable the generalization of existing theorems concerning the additive properties of functions in specific sequences and facilitate their practical application. For instance, this could elucidate the underlying mechanisms of the additive properties of functions in the Walnut and Walsh near exponential sequences, which were demonstrated to be false in this paper. For example, if characterizing group-theoretic near exponential sequences in $\mathbb{Z}$ becomes possible, it could provide a foundation for characterizing those in the $\mathbb{N}$-based near exponential sequences mentioned earlier

By applying a timeodd Carnahan-Hamilton-Nelson-Norton tensor, the model constructs odd-nucleus pairing energies from these even-even quantities. To improve the mass surface learning, an artificial and physically unmotivated charge $Z^2$ learning term is employed. Although this additional loss function lacks physical justification, it significantly enhances the model's ability to pair odd-nucleus energies with even-even nucleon pairings. Consequently, the resulting mass residual root-mean-square deviation of $0.644 \, \text{MeV}$ regarding $208$ even-even nuclei aligns with other modern parameterized even-even nucleon pairing models and contradicts direct experimental measurements of nuclear binding energies by $35$ to $40 \, \text{MeV}$. These findings indicate that Bayesian neural networks represent a promising machine learning approach for modeling nuclear binding energies. Furthermore, the mass surface and pairing energy formulations developed here establish a foundation for investigating other phenomena governed by nucleon compositions, such as the location of the island of stability for superheavy elements and the proton drip radius. Additionally, the model demonstrates a $95\%$ accuracy rate in predicting $\beta$-decay half-lives by utilizing established even-even nucleon pairing rules to account for neutron-rich and proton-rich decay channels. Finally, the research demonstrates that the use of a tensor alongside an artificial learning term offers a viable pathway for machine learning models to accurately predict odd-nucleus pairing energies. Conventional exact techniques, such as Benders decomposition and column-and-constraint generation, address this by solving mixed-integer linear programs (MILP) to locate extreme points of feasible sets or objective value sets. However, these standard methods suffer from two primary drawbacks. First, when the number of possible parameter realizations is large, the resulting MILPs can become unwieldy even within seemingly simple settings. Second, these techniques can fail completely for unbounded objective function sets, which occurs, for instance, when the second-stage objective coefficients rely on parameter realizations. We overcome these limitations by proposing an algorithm that evaluates the plausibility of each parameter realization based on its distance from the support set and the reach of its confidence level, incorporating both first- and second-stage objectives within a single optimization model. Our numerical experiments indicate that, across various instances, these new methods significantly outperform traditional exact approaches in terms of computational efficiency, particularly when dealing with numerous parameter realizations. Additionally, experimental results using diverse datasets demonstrate that the proposed algorithm can enhance the solution quality of standard heuristic approaches. to digital footprints, which encompass various traces of individual digital activity accessible to tech giants, often termed "big data." Driven by their vast scale, these traces support numerous social, economic, and socioeconomic applications, including poverty prediction. Yet, little attention has been given to the mechanisms behind these transformations, specifically regarding claims that digital footprints enable accurate and fair prediction. This study employs a quasi-experimental design to address this gap. By leveraging a natural experiment in Brazil involving a nationwide census and a unified database of digital footprints, we assessed the accuracy and fairness of a leading poverty prediction system. Our findings indicate that while digital footprints indeed facilitate accurate poverty prediction, they do so in a highly discriminatory manner. Furthermore, we identified the specific information elements responsible for this bias and demonstrated that eliminating them significantly enhances fairness without substantially reducing accuracy. Ultimately, our results highlight the necessity of critically evaluating how and why digital footprints drive socioeconomic applications, urging policymakers, developers, and tech executives to prioritize fairness alongside accuracy in such systems. Furthermore, we advocate for smaller, more interpretable data sources over those characterized by an overwhelming volume of information. This research underscores the imperative for interdisciplinary collaboration between computer science and social science, aiming to foster more responsible innovations in artificial intelligence and machine learning. We further seek to foster a broader dialogue concerning ethical guidelines and necessary policies that can safeguard human rights and societal well-being. Finally, we provide a comprehensive dataset featuring detailed explanations and visualizations, alongside links to all corresponding source codes. We anticipate this will serve as a valuable resource for scholars and practitioners interested in ethical issues within AI and machine learning. In summary, this work illustrates that even when digital data enables precise predictions, it need not be discriminatory, thereby opening new avenues for more ethical and accountable data-driven applications across various domains. INTRODUCTION Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are increasingly applied across various computer science disciplines, including software engineering, graph mining, and network analysis. GNNs have gained traction in recent years due to their robust performance on complex graph-structured data, making them particularly suitable for energy system applications. Energy systems typically consist of multiple interconnected components, such as generators, transformers, and transmission lines, which can be effectively represented as graphs. Moreover, the inherent stochasticity of renewable energy sources can be captured by the messaging structures between system components, which mirror the topological connections within the network. GNNs leverage these message-passing relationships to learn from the system's topology, thereby addressing the limitations of traditional neural networks. This section introduces graph concepts and outlines the motivation and background for applying GNNs to energy systems. Graph Concepts A graph is a collection of nodes representing entities, where edges signify relationships between them. A graph $G$ is formally defined as a pair $(V, E)$, where $V$ denotes the set of nodes (vertices) and $E$ represents the set of edges connecting them. Edges can be directed or undirected; when the relationship between nodes is symmetric, the resulting graph is considered undirected. Edge attributes provide additional information about the connections between nodes.

While this approach is highly effective for regular users with substantial activity logs, it fails to suggest relevant items for new users with limited or no interaction history. To solve this, the proposed Ising Model Collaborative Filtering (IMCF) integrates collaborative filtering with the Predecessor-Complementary recommendation strategy. This method models a new user's interactions with items as the thermodynamic ground state of an Ising model, effectively combining user-item activity history with item attributes to generate personalized suggestions. Empirical results demonstrate that IMCF outperforms traditional collaborative filtering by increasing the precision of recommended items. Furthermore, numerical analysis indicates that even in scenarios relying solely on item attributes (without collaborative filtering), the model achieves significant recommendation accuracy by identifying ground state configurations that align well with observed observations. Additionally, simulation studies show that IMCF remains effective in handling missing interaction data. Finally, it has been established that finding ground state configurations for the Ising model is computationally intractable; consequently, an approximate algorithm for IMCF is developed incorporating a simulated annealing-based local search. This approach successfully identifies appropriate items for user recommendations even when only partial attribute information is available. Additionally, it is numerically verified that these recommended items are compatible with existing items held by the user. By addressing the cold-start problem more effectively than conventional collaborative filtering methods, IMCF is expected to enhance the user experience. Furthermore, the applicability of Ising model-based machine learning to machine learning combined with deep neural network hybrid architectures opens new possibilities for creating next-generation intelligent recommendation systems. Furthermore, the framework's extensibility allows for the easy inclusion of additional user and item features, facilitating the construction of even more refined recommendation models. Consequently, Ising model-based machine learning holds significant potential for the future development of intelligent recommendation systems. Recently, highly doped, atomically thin, single-layer WSe$_2$ (tungsten selenide) has been demonstrated to exhibit a finite energy gap, indicating a topological insulating (TI) state. In this study, we investigate how a substrate-induced out-of-plane strain affects this topological phase. Our mean-field analysis of the spin-orbit-coupling (SOC)-split band structure, using experimentally derived parameters from the subgap region, shows that compressive strain (where $\varepsilon > 0$) reduces the energy gap by modifying the crystal potential. Furthermore, a critical strain threshold of $\varepsilon_{c} = 1.35\%$ is identified. When this limit is reached, the gap closes and the TI phase transitions into a metallic state. These findings are corroborated by many-body $G_0W_0$ calculations based on a $U$-corrected Kohn-Sham (KS) band structure of highly doped WSe$_2$. Additionally, we examine the strain sensitivity of the TI phase through the low-energy density of states. Ultimately, we establish that the strain tolerance for the topological phase in WSe$_2$ does not exceed $\varepsilon_{c} = 1.35\%$. Finally, the impact of the backside substrate on the TI phase is analyzed by comparing results from mean-field and many-body theories. This sensitivity analysis serves to set upper bounds on the strain tolerance required to maintain the topological phase integrity in device applications. Our computational results indicate that the backside substrate must be rigid and smooth to ensure the stability of the topological phase. These findings provide a foundation for the practical implementation of topological devices using 2D materials. First, for any cover $P: P\to B$ and any subgroup $H$ of the base space $B$, we demonstrate the existence of a unique "maximal" cover $P':P\to B'$ that restricts to $P$ over $B\setminus H$, thereby solving an extension problem for $P$. Covering spaces and their generalizations play crucial roles in various fields, including topology, group theory, and non-topological homotopy theory. Finally, each homomorphism $h:G\to P$ yields a "strongest" partial homotopy that covers it. These optimal partial homotopies are essential for defining the bicomplex associated with a cover $P: P\to B$ (introduced by Biss in 2002) and its generalization, the bicomplex of a cover and a subgroup. This study provides a statistical mechanical framework for understanding these Pauli crystals by computing key parameters of the resulting lattice. By incorporating the effects of non-interaction and finite temperature, we derive the chemical potential and the spacing between adjacent fermion layers for the ground state lattice. At temperatures where the thermal de Broglie wavelength remains significantly smaller than the layer spacing, the predicted distance between the first two fermion layers aligns with results from numerical simulations. Comparing the scale of the Pauli crystal's lattice spacing with the radius of a typical neutron star reveals that a uniform distribution of neutrons remains more realistic. Nevertheless, the derived expression for the Pauli exclusion distance could aid in exploring the complex relationship between neutrons in the core and those on the surface of a neutron star. *   We present a mathematical method to assess the impact of reflections on a camera's utility as an artificial lighting source.
*   Utilizing a mathematical camera model, we quantify how object reflectance affects a camera's potential as an illumination source considering its spectral characteristics.
*   Based on this analysis, we propose a solution to automatically select an appropriate filter for the primary camera.
*   We validate the approach on real-world datasets, demonstrating that image quality correlates directly with our derived diffusion quality metric.
*   The methodology is validated in a practical application involving the lighting setup for a scanning system. We demonstrate that a neural network trained using our proposed solution achieves superior results compared to those trained on unfiltered camera setups. This validation utilizes a real-world dataset available at https://github.com/ESL-2021-Team-11/estimated-diffusion-quality-.

This approach utilizes simulated lenslet arrays to model wavefront sampling via quad-cell detectors on the mirrors. By representing mirror segments as highly parameterized shapes, we can efficiently explore shape-space to determine optimal configurations. For initial assessments, we evaluated subring focus mirrors arranged in a 4x4 grid, optimizing them to minimize wavefront sampling errors during observation of a circular off-axis source. Results indicate that after several thousand iterations, the total squared error from ideal quad-cell responses drops below 1%. However, the method encounters difficulties when sampling areas near the mirror edges. Ongoing efforts explore strategies to address this boundary issue; one potential solution involves applying a mask to the edges prior to wavefront sampling. A secondary objective addresses the challenge of refocusing swished streaks following gamma-radiation damage to the secondary mirror's multilayer coating. Simulations demonstrate that if the radiation-induced change in the streak's width can be accurately measured on the focal plane sensors, a concave quadratically parameterized shape can restore the linearity of wavefront sampling. In both applications, the optimization methodology proves highly effective for initial assessments, though more comprehensive and more highly parameterized studies are warranted. Ultimately, optimization of X-ray mirror shapes for off-axis observation represents a promising application of mirror parameterization, offering a straightforward path to improve modeling and wavefront-sampling strategies for future wide-field X-ray telescopes. Additionally, the development of a refocusable secondary mirror presents a novel approach to mitigating radiation damage in X-ray telescopes. These findings suggest numerous future applications, including the optimization of currently unrefocused mirrors, secondary mirror parameterization for wide-field instruments utilizing focused mirrors, and strategies for characterizing radiation-damaged mirrors. Furthermore, this research could facilitate the exploration of previously unexamined mirror designs. Ultimately, these outcomes will aid in establishing a framework for characterizing and managing radiation damage in future X-ray telescopes. In this study, we investigate a topologically non-trivial model that breaks periodic boundary conditions, specifically within a Fd3m Weyl semimetal. This framework generates a novel form of topological protection where the quantum Hall effect emerges without relying on crystal momentum, utilizing instead the translation operator as the primary operator. This range is termed "quasi-periodic" topological theory. We demonstrate that, under open boundary conditions, the bulk gap states form equidistant towers of translation-momentum eigenstates located at band edges when the magnetic field is applied along the [111] direction. We provide a systematic method for calculating the topological invariants known as "translation quantum numbers" and experimentally observe these number changes as the magnetic field intensity varies. These findings may offer a new perspective for investigating systems that lack Bloch symmetry. Additionally, we propose that quasi-momentum can be redefined via path integrals of the wave function under periodic boundary conditions, which can be accessed through quantum measurements of translation operators. This research paves the way for exploring topological phenomena in systems that do not adhere to Bloch's theorem. More significantly, our findings hold high promise for characterizing the bulk properties of materials using angular-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), even when atoms lack well-defined centers. Such a theoretical framework could potentially be extended to other systems, including quasi-crystals, moiré materials, and cold-atom systems. Our predictions can be validated using existing equipment at synchrotron radiation sources, such as the National Synchrotron Radiation Laboratory in Hefei, China. entropy into the solar atmosphere: magnetic reconnection and the ambipolar diffusion term. These processes are modeled using a 3D magnetohydrodynamic framework that incorporates ambipolar diffusion, driven by the lack of charge neutrality in the upper atmosphere, alongside the double layer model of magnetic reconnection, which relies on electron cooling. Both mechanisms generate entropic effects at a scale smaller than the scale height, creating a step-function-like entropy distribution across an intermediate scale. This results in a power spectrum decay proportional to $k^{-1}$ at high wavenumbers, regardless of the relative strength of each mechanism, a conclusion supported by turbulence simulations. Although ambipolar diffusion is the primary contributor to energy dissipation, magnetic reconnection creates a locally high entropy region that spreads via binary splitting, governed by the inverse cascade of enstrophy. This drives an intermittent energy release, manifesting as a slight deviation from the $k^{-1}$ decay and introducing an additional slope increase in the power spectrum, characteristic of turbulent cascades with finite-resolved entropic interfaces. This phenomenon may represent the origin of low-frequency solar oscillations. Finally, we propose an alternative explanation for the $k^{-5/3}$ power spectrum decay, which is crucial for the solar wind, without requiring an intermediate cascade. This final power spectrum arises from the interaction between the two entropic interfaces and enstrophy during the turbulence state, marking a significant advancement in understanding energy dissipation in magnetized turbulent plasmas. This understanding is derived from our analysis of the nonlinear stage of the Riemann problem, which represents the initial condition of the system. The study presents the initial formulation of this problem and reports its first numerical solution. These findings may aid in understanding coronal heating, solar wind acceleration, and microturbulence in the corona and upper atmosphere. Solar Physics, Vol. 235, pp. 367--398, 2008. This data will offer unprecedented depth and breadth for monitoring the sky across diverse wavelengths, including UV, optical, near-IR, and submillimeter radiation. These observations will be supported by numerous cosmology-focused telescopes, both ground-based and space-based, that utilize transient surveys as part of their primary or secondary objectives. This review outlines the physics behind various transient sources and the methods used to study them. It outlines strategies for multimeessenger and multi-wavelength follow-up using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and Simons Observatory SOO/CTA, highlighting their significant potential for multi-wavelength analysis. A key finding is the possibility of using these facilities to investigate the physical nature of certain rare transients, such as Type-Ib/c supernovae, TDEs, and GRBs, which currently lack near-IR follow-up data from JWST. Furthermore, we demonstrate the value of near-IR observations in distinguishing between specific transient classes, such as Type-IIP and II-L supernovae. Finally, we emphasize the importance of optical and near-IR data for verifying gravitational wave sources and the role of transient surveys in discovering strongly lensed cosmological events. These tasks require extensive all-sky coverage to detect and monitor the high number of expected transients. Furthermore, we show that JWST can significantly enhance optical/near-IR follow-up capabilities for cosmological time-delay lensing through precise astrometry and high spectral resolution. In summary, our research indicates that a comprehensive study of optical/near-IR transients, accompanied by JWST follow-up, represents a highly effective strategy for advancing astrophysics and cosmology within the current all-sky transient survey landscape. This approach will ensure maximum utilization of the anticipated data deluge from the LSST. Future research will provide a more detailed assessment of the scientific potential for astrophysics and cosmology, specifically focusing on time-delay cosmology. In both scenarios, n elements must be selected to maximize the total value of chosen elements, subject to a constraint that the count of selected elements from any specific group must not exceed the size of that group. Unlike the traditional Knapsack Problem, which is NP-hard, both SUKP and BMCP admit polynomial-time solvability. However, cycling presents safety risks, and numerous countries have seen a rise in accidental bicycle deaths. Our goal is to promote cycling while maintaining user safety by enabling them to detect impending collisions with moving vehicles. This can be achieved through equipping bicycles with onboard sensors that continuously monitor the surroundings. We propose a sensor fusion system that integrates data from multiple sensors to establish a real-time framework for collision avoidance. By employing probabilistic fusion techniques, we track moving vehicles despite the noisy and uncertain signals produced by the sensors. The system is adaptable to various bicycle shapes and built-environments, making it suitable for both urban and rural settings. We have developed a mathematical model to process signals from several sensors and have successfully implemented this model using a camera and a sonar sensor on a bicycle prototype. We demonstrate that this proposed system, termed BeCySaR (an acronym for Bicycle Safety and Reliable Autonomy), can achieve significant accuracy in predicting vehicle future positions and alert riders to potential crashes. As a motivating case study, we applied this framework to avoiding a car crash in an urban setting. We captured the bicycle's position and orientation using a 2D camera and measured distances to obstacles with a sonar sensor, processing over 20,000 frames in real-time. This framework enables riders to foresee accidents and take preventive action. We illustrate the system's performance in predicting future vehicle positions and the time remaining before a potential crash. We also present experimental results from two real-world accidents where the system alerted the rider in time to prevent impact. BeCySaR offers riders enough time to execute evasive maneuvers or reduce speed to avoid crashing against large vehicles. This system holds significant value for riders of all experience levels, from experts to those new to cycling. We believe this technology will substantially reduce accidents and fatalities among riders. Finally, we propose that regulators and industry leaders require such systems as a mandatory feature for all bicycles. Without such regulation, we fear that accidents and rider deaths will continue to increase. It is crucial to shift public perception by demonstrating that cycling can be as safe as driving a car. We contend that BeCySaR will help change these perceptions. Additionally, we show that the system remains effective during the day with or without specific lighting. When such a cover exists, the covering number $\sigma(R)$ denotes the cardinality of a minimal cover. A ring $R$ is defined as $\sigma$-elementary if $\sigma(R) < \sigma(R/I)$ for every nonzero two-sided ideal $I$. This paper presents the first instances of $\sigma$-elementary rings $R$ possessing a nonzero two-sided ideal $I$ such that $\sigma(R) = \sigma(R/I) + 1$, specifically within contexts where $R$ is a finite direct sum of copies of the quaternions over a field or an algebraic division ring. Consequently, these rings have a zero nilpotent radical and a zero lower unitization covering number. These findings resolve several open problems recently identified by Berman, Petkovšek, and Traotape (2021). Furthermore, the study characterizes the covers of such quaternions and demonstrates that, unlike most other known examples of $\sigma$-elementary rings, they do not possess a maximal subring that is not a cover. Berman, Petkovšek, and Traotape previously demonstrated that if $R$ is a finite direct sum of rings, then $\sigma(R) \geq \frac{3}{4}\sigma(R_0)$, where $R_0$ is the subring of $R$ comprising elements with zero components in all non-uniform positions. These new examples achieve the theoretical lower bound of $\sigma(R_0)$ established by Berman, Petkovšek, and Traotape for finite direct sums of unital rings. Additionally, the cover structure of these quaternions minimizes the sum of the covers of their coordinate rings, reaching the lower bound of $\sigma(R_0) + \sigma(R_1)$. Finally, the covering numbers of these quaternions are calculated for all possible characteristic $p$ of the underlying commutative ring $R_0$. The analysis reveals that when $p=2$, the coordinate rings are maximal subrings; however, when $p$ is an odd prime, the cover structure becomes more complex, as not all covers consist of maximal subrings. Despite this complexity, the covering numbers remain consistent across both scenarios. In particular models featuring local symmetry breaking, the classical Lipschitz continuity of solutions is generally absent; instead, data singularities inevitably develop. This study presents a novel, fully explicit numerical algorithm designed to approximate such solutions while naturally adhering to an entropy condition necessary for selecting the physically relevant admissible solution. The fully discrete scheme guarantees stability within the energy framework and converges energy-stable to the weak entropy solution, even in the presence of singularities. Furthermore, the scheme fully discretizes the concept of relative entropy, thereby providing a discrete formulation of the entropy condition. These theoretical findings are supported by a selection of numerical experiments. These examples illustrate both the formation of singularities and the capability of the scheme to capture the dynamical process of local symmetry breaking. The location and asymptotic behavior of emerging data singularities are precisely predicted by the asymptotic analysis of the discrete energy's gradient. Additionally, the discrete formulation enables the construction of the nonlocal Lipschitz constant on singularities and facilitates the use of the scheme for addressing free boundary problems. These advancements are demonstrated through a numerical investigation of a numerical boundary condition derived from the Lewis-Weinstein-Weiss Lewis Lewis-Weiss model, which supports local symmetry breaking.

This paper investigates open dynamical questions regarding these surfaces, specifically focusing on the density of orbits. We demonstrate that for a dense set of arbitrary dilation surfaces, the stable unbounded orbits associated with the dilation surface action coincide. This finding contrasts sharply with classical dilation surfaces like $\delta$-Lattices, where the action yields divergent geodesics and $\delta$ varies for each surface. Our approach relies on reducing general dilation surfaces to specific, well-understood models known as right-angled hexagons. The proof establishes two key results: first, that a dense collection of arithmetic hexagons forms a single divergent class; and second, that a specific set of asymptotic dilation surfaces, which are built from finite iterated extensions of well-chosen asymptotic hexagons, also constitutes a single divergent class. Since the divergence of the former group is already established in the literature, the divergence of the latter follows directly. These findings are derived by continuously shifting between different geometric and algebraic models rather than making discrete transitions between them. The study of right-angled hexagons is the primary innovation of this research, with a dedicated section exploring their novel divergent geometry. Building upon this concept, this study infers a whole-brain connectivity network using Total Correlation and demonstrates its potential as a biomarker for distinguishing Alzheimer's Disease (AD) from Control (Control) cohorts. This work explores how this framework extends to general Hamiltonians that are either multiplication or Hamilton vector fields on the phase space of the Bargmann manifold. We introduce a novel model featuring a one-parameter family of unitary representations for the Heisenberg algebra, which encompasses the classical Segal-Bargmann representation as a specific instance. To characterize the Hilbert space of this representation, we construct an explicit orthonormal basis using Hermite polynomials modified to align with the dynamics of general Hamiltonians. Furthermore, we examine the conditions required for the representation to be irreducible and offer several applications of our findings within the canonical quantization program. Specifically, in the context of the Weyl-Wigner-Goyal quantization method, we demonstrate that geometric states corresponding to non-degenerate, constant-curvature Hamiltonian vector fields map to Dirac deltas, while those associated with multiplication functions yield zero. Additionally, in an appendix, we provide a cohomological proof establishing the Hilbert space isomorphism between quantum mechanics with distinct Hamiltonians. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the Weyl-Wigner-Goyal quantization successfully navigates the ultraviolet divergence problem, a conclusion supported by an example of a quantum state representing the quantized version of the Cauchy kernel in complex analysis, whose associated Wigner function exhibits no singularities. This effect stems from the fact that Wigner functions in this theory possess a lower effective dimension than their classical counterparts. In a numerical investigation, we analyze the evolution of the quantum state representing the Cauchy kernel; although not an eigenstate, it behaves effectively as such, with its Wigner function representing the quantum equivalent of the Cauchy integral formula. Through the Weyl-Wigner-Goyal lens, the quantum mechanics of the Cauchy kernel reveals elegant features linked to complex analysis, offering promising avenues for future research. Furthermore, in another appendix, we consider a model representing the quantum mechanics of the Fock representation of the Heisenberg algebra, where Wigner functions for specific states correspond to the quantum versions of Poisson brackets, with implications in number theory. Finally, in a computational framework, the quantum states representing the Cauchy kernel serve as eigenstates for a self-adjoint, positive-definite operator. The associated Wigner functions provide a coarse-grained approximation of the spectral density for the positive integers. The research is pertinent to applications such as Wi-Fi enabled public safety radio systems operating in the 5 GHz band (specifically DSS and TDD modes), as well as wireless communications in military, medical, scientific, and educational sectors utilizing various radio standards (including UWB, MRU, GMSK, and LoRa) also in the 5G band, notably GMSK-LoRa interoperability. Data was collected using a custom-built outdoor test bed in an uncluttered area, featuring two half-wave dipole antennas aligned horizontally at a distance of 22 meters. Transmitted powers of 15 mW and 100 mW were employed, with receivers positioned at heights ranging from 0.3 to 2.4 meters. Measurements were conducted under two conditions: antennas mounted on tripods and antennas held at waist height. Results indicate that when antennas are near the ground, significant fading occurs at certain heights, causing deviations from the Two-Ray model. However, when receivers are elevated above a specific height, the model accurately forecasts received power, and two distinct zones with consistent path loss exponents are identified. This study provides precise estimates for the threshold separating these zones. Additionally, the path loss exponents were determined to be 3.06 and 3.08 for the specific frequencies and antenna heights used. These findings suggest that the two-Ray model's applicability depends on receiver height; it is valid only when the height exceeds a specific threshold, which in this specific setup is approximately 1.6 meters. Under a specific control policy, the expected cost-to-go at any state is defined as the fixed point of a Bellman operator, and a Q-function is introduced to represent the expected difference in cost-to-go resulting from a control action at a specific state and time. While numerous methods have been proposed for this task, they often rely on restrictive assumptions or are tailored to specific ST-PL problems, limiting their generalizability. To address this, we introduce a general framework that leverages pre-training to capture both local and global dependencies within video sequences and infer them in new tasks. Furthermore, we validate the framework's effectiveness across various ST-PL tasks, including video compression, animation, and video forensics. This concept is now extended to pre-transformed polar codes, such as CRC-aided polar codes, which previously lacked the automorphisms necessary for permutation decoding. By employing belief propagation (BP) as the pre-transform, we establish a framework that enhances performance through error pattern selection and improves robustness via the combination of symmetric code permutations and iterative BP. Furthermore, we adapt the recently developed successive cancellation cancellation (SCC) decoding algorithm, which utilizes pre-decoding operations to reduce decoding complexity. Experimental results indicate that permutation decoding yields significant benefits across various code lengths and failure rates. Specifically, for a $(2, 2046, 1963)$ CRC-aided polar code, permutation decoding achieves a gain of approximately $\rm 0.45~dB$ at a word error rate ($\mathrm{WER}$) of $10^{-4}$ compared to successive cancellation list (SCL) decoding with pre-decoding, while exhibiting a more favorable trade-off between $\mathrm{WER}$ and decoding complexity. When applied to a $(2, 3072, 1024)$ polar code designed for the 5G short packet regime, permutation decoding improves performance by approximately $\rm 0.22~dB$ over iterative BP-SCL at an $\mathrm{WER}$ of $10^{-5}$, with a minimal increase in decoding complexity. Additionally, permutation decoding facilitates a higher degree of parallelism compared to standard SCL. For the 2048-length code, it reduces the decoding time required to achieve a $\mathrm{WER}$ of $10^{-4}$ by $\rm 0.07~dB$ in simulations, representing a $\rm 2.1\times$ speedup. Furthermore, permutation decoding enables a $\rm 2.0\times$ reduction in decoding time while maintaining the same $\mathrm{WER}$ for the 5G short packet code. These promising outcomes suggest that permutation decoding is well-suited for deployment in 5G short packet communication systems. (See https://arxiv.org/pdf/2002.00920 for the arXiv source.) Beginning with statistical mechanics, we incorporate "contact physics" to derive the laws governing contact mechanics, which serve as the foundation of our framework. These laws specify bulk properties and boundary conditions, enabling us to transition directly to the second law of thermodynamics. Leveraging the scaling law, we re-examine the Navier-Stokes equation to introduce key modifications. To model density, we employ both statistical mechanics and the Radial Distribution Function (RDF). To represent the order parameter, we derive the Q tensor from RDF data using mesoscale averaging. To address the stress tensor, we derive the active Stokes equation from the second law of thermodynamics. Finally, by decomposing vector fields into irrotational and solenoidal components, we interpret the third law of thermodynamics and its associated scaling law to formulate the governing equations for active matter. This approach successfully explains the second and third laws, which were previously misunderstood in the context of active matter, and provides a complete, concise, and logically consistent set of governing equations. These equations are demonstrated to align with the 2D active nematic model (ANM) through specific examples. Additionally, we propose a novel, general approach for deriving the RDF from a free energy density function (Ginzburg-Landau type), ensuring compatibility. By focusing on bulk contact properties and boundary conditions, this method is also expected to be applicable to other contact problems. Ultimately, the resulting equations offer a promising foundation for the design and engineering of active matter systems. This methodology represents a significant advancement in the understanding of fundamental physics in this field. Most significantly, the proposed framework offers a promising avenue for the future understanding of active matter physics. Recently, Mahaffee et al. introduced an interactive proof of quantum knowledge (POK) scheme enabling a server to demonstrate knowledge of a quantum state $\psi$ prepared via an quantum random access memory (QRAM). Building on this, our research focuses on enhancing the classical client within this setting. First, we present a more straightforward verification method for the quantum state POK by Mahaffee et al., achieving a reduced number of classical operations while maintaining the same knowledge soundness parameter. Second, we propose a quantum server construction where the knowledge soundness parameter depends on the security of the quantum state rather than the state's size. To achieve this, we develop a novel QRAM scheme that minimizes the quantum processing units required per entry in the quantum program. This optimization facilitates the verification of larger-scale quantum programs. Finally, through classical and quantum simulation, we compare our approach with the original POK scheme and other related methods. The results indicate that our scheme offers superior knowledge soundness compared to existing schemes. Crucially, unlike other methods, our scheme verifies larger programs more efficiently by reducing the quantum resources needed for state preparation. The trade-off is a slightly higher cost for the classical client. We conclude that our scheme represents a new optimization pathway for verifying quantum computation. While prior work has relied on ellipsoids to model cellular geometry, this paper introduces a more versatile framework for generating cell shapes. We present the radial shape parameterization (ReShP), a system that maps a set of vertices to a set of radii defining the desired form. A single unique quadric surface is derived for each ReShP instance, enabling efficient rendering across various applications. The approach is versatile and extensible; its flexibility allows for the representation of diverse shapes, including convex and complex cells with caveolae. Furthermore, reparameterization techniques can be employed to produce smooth, realistic, and biologically plausible forms. ReShP instances adhere to a canonical geometry, ensuring that shapes along a transformation are preserved, parallel transport is maintained, and topological shifts can be tracked to map transformed vertices back to their original positions. We demonstrate the technique's utility by applying it to simulate several common cellular phenomena, such as proliferation, migration, apoptosis, and infection. Finally, we provide a R package to support the replication and expansion of this research. AC have identified a class of protoplanetary disks characterized by extreme inner cavity truncation, with only a minute fraction of material located outside the water snowline, a feature often linked to active planet formation. However, this scenario is at odds with current theories of planet and dust evolution in passive disks. This study proposes an alternative interpretation: these systems may not be typical stage III water-deprived disks but rather stage II stages featuring a central cavity formed by dust growth and radial drift within a snow-rich environment. We illustrate this hypothesis using the TW Hya disk as a representative example. Under this framework, the radio continuum emission originates from free-free radiation produced by ionized material (such as water) in a circumstellar region, while the 13CO emission arises from collisionally excited molecules within the disk's outer layers. This configuration offers a consistent explanation for the observed inner radio continuum, continuum, and gas emission profiles, as well as the depletion of dust in the inner cavity. Specifically, we calculate that a water-rich zone between 1 and 20 AU must contain approximately 1.1 M$_\oplus$ of water to match the observed radio continuum flux. Our model also accounts for the lack of mid-IR emission from TW Hya's cavity, the recent detection of inner dust via dust-plasma interactions, and predictions for future observations of the central cavity at shorter wavelengths. This mechanism provides an efficient and rapid method for depositing water onto outer disks, potentially facilitating planet formation. Furthermore, we apply this model to other cavity-bearing disks, including HD 100453, SAO 20646, D24-141, M1629, and Sz39e, demonstrating that their observed emission spectra can be explained if water-rich regions exist within approximately 100 AU. The frequent detection of such regions by JWST/NIRSpec IFU supports the validity of this hypothesis. We conclude that the presence of a water-deprived inner cavity is not a prerequisite for planet formation; instead, stage II disks exhibiting inner cavity truncation may serve as promising candidates for forming planets.

This study examines the alteration in the electron gas dimensionality—from feature-free two-dimensional surfaces to features with a nanometer scale—by analyzing systems where the Fermi wavelength is smaller than the system size. We investigate rectangular graphene sheets of varying nanometer dimensions to understand how the ground state evolves from a bulk 2D metal to a zero-dimensional quantum dot. Furthermore, we show that the ground state excitation energy and energy gaps can be tuned across this spectrum by adjusting the nanometer size. Additionally, we illustrate the impact of zero-dimensional confinement on work function modifications across different state regimes. These findings may assist in interpreting experimental data regarding junctions connecting nanometer-sized entities to bulk solids. Ultimately, our results provide a computational pathway to potentially enhance the work function of materials for use in field electron emitters and photovoltaic applications. Additionally, given the potential magnetic nature of these quantum dot states in graphene, it is possible to further adjust the work function by applying an external magnetic field. Additionally, our findings suggest that the work function in zero-dimensional regimes is sensitive to the shape of the potential well; thus, modifying the well's shape offers a method for further tuning the work function. Collectively, our findings open new avenues for ground state investigations in nanometer-sized conductors. Moreover, our research paves the way for utilizing nanometer-sized junctions as a ground state tool to systematically modify the work function. This ability to tune the work function could facilitate the development of highly efficient field electron emitters and novel laser technologies. Finally, our work function calculations in this quantum regime may facilitate further theoretical and experimental research into the ground state properties of nanometer-sized junctions. We first analyze the delay-independent stability of the disease-free equilibrium for both continuous and discrete models, demonstrating that immunity type (continuous vs. discrete) does not impact asymptotic stability. Subsequently, we establish delay-independent stability for the positive invariant set specific to each age group. Finally, we investigate the stability characteristics regarding the number of generations within the model featuring pure age structure. These findings are supported by numerical examples. Through numerical analysis, we introduce and examine several biological interpretations encompassing local stability, delay-independent stability, and stability with respect to the number of generations. Our results indicate that delay-independent stability does not require the imposition of additional restrictions on model parameters. Additionally, we prove that stable age density specific to each age group does not generate periodic solutions in the time-delayed model, irrespective of whether immunity is natural or acquired, nor does it influence the existence of age density and its stability. This represents the first investigation into delay-independent stability in age-structured epidemic models. Furthermore, we propose a novel methodology for analyzing stability with respect to the number of generations in this context. These conclusions are significant and may prove valuable for public health policy, particularly in nations where most infections occur among the young. More broadly, this research offers new insights into understanding various age-related infectious diseases. Additionally, it opens new avenues for future studies on stability criteria for epidemic models with age structure. We also present two future research directions: [1] investigating other biological properties of age-structured epidemic models, and [2] developing age-dependent epidemic models that include the spread of misinformation. These proposals are based on our age density stability findings and the observation that the total infected population does not converge to zero in age-structured models. We believe this research offers new perspectives for future investigations into age-structured epidemic models. More than 20 years have passed since the initial publication on age-structured epidemic models [1], and given the current global pandemic, the need for such research remains highly relevant. While previous studies [2–8] have utilized age density to investigate epidemic models, this paper offers new insights by employing age density-specific positive invariant sets to investigate age-structured models with time delays. This approach yields more refined stability criteria compared to previous works [2–8]. More broadly, it also presents new insights into age-structured epidemic models. More specifically, it provides additional biological interpretations of age density and unique stability criteria for age-structured epidemic models. Specifically, we demonstrate decidability for extensions defined by infinitary hyperatomic congruential axioms, which encompass all recursively axiomatizable superextensions of classical propositional logic. Additionally, we establish that decidability holds for extensions formed by infinitary modular axioms. It is already recognized that the finite axiomatizable superextension, proposed by Paoli in 2014 and defined by axioms F1 and F2, is an infinitary hyperatomic congruential axiomatic extension; we prove its decidability as a specific instance of our main findings. In this section, we also examine Paoli's other proposed superextension, which requires axioms F3 and F4, and demonstrate that it is not modular. Finally, we confirm that the axiomatic extension defined by the infinite set of axioms $\{ \alpha \to \bigvee_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \alpha^n \}$—an axiomatic version of the multiplicative axiom from affine logic—is an example of a non-decidable extension, as it is neither supercongruential nor modular. The core of our decidability results for superextensions relies on the existence of finite characteristic matrices and supermatrices derived from them. These matrices and supermatrices are constructed from a finite matrix where each valuation assigns to every formula a vector of finite length, representing the images of all infinite valuations within a specific variety as defined by the axioms. We also show that every superextension with a finite axial variety admits a finite characteristic matrix. The non-decidability argument, conversely, relies on the existence of filter-atomic filters, a property derived from Makinson's (1986) characterization of varieties with projective varieties of filters via matroid axioms. By combining this result with existing mathematical theorems, we can identify varieties of algebras whose axiomatic extensions are non-decidable. Furthermore, we present a generalization of this approach to prove the undecidability of certain axiomatic extensions defined by infinitary co-Herbrand axioms. Keyboards are essential input devices for computers, yet they are predominantly designed for writing in natural languages rather than for interacting with other computer-based technologies. This paper explores whether taxonomies can serve as effective mediating input methods between users and computer systems. Specifically, we investigate: (1) if taxonomy navigation can facilitate quicker access to less frequent concepts compared to alphabetic keyboards, (2) if concept labels can be more intuitive than hierarchical structure, and (3) if hierarchical structure can be effectively rendered through keyboard input. Through a series of studies, we assessed users' proficiency with taxonomy navigation for inputting rare words, concepts associated with varying label and hierarchy structures, and found that taxonomy navigation performed no better than alphabetic keyboards. Additionally, lexical features proved more significant than hierarchical structures in influencing input method performance. Keyboards featuring hierarchical structures incurred excessive cognitive overhead for most participants. These findings may assist in designing novel input techniques that leverage rich hierarchical data rather than simple linear lists. Code and data are available at https://github.com/cmu-plglab/keyboards-for-taxonomies.

Through quantitative analysis, the influence of weak magnetism on the electric dipole moment of $\Xi_b^0$ is assessed. Findings indicate that inclusion of weak magnetism amplifies the electric dipole moment by approximately one order of magnitude relative to its contribution from charge asymmetry alone. These outcomes underscore that the electric dipole moment of $\Xi_b^0$ serves as a potent tool for investigating T-violation in the decay of bottom-containing six-quark systems. Additionally, the analysis of the ratio $\mathcal{R}_D$ between the electric dipole moments of $\Xi_b^0$ and $\Xi_c^0$ offers further insights into the potential of six-quark systems for studying T-violation. Given that $\mathcal{R}_D$ remains relatively invariant against variations in hadronic parameters and wave function configurations, it mitigates uncertainties arising from QCD matrix element calculations, thereby facilitating the measurement of $\Xi_b^-\to\Xi^0\pi^-$ decays at LHCb. This research further recommends that the LHCb experimental group intensify efforts to search for an electric dipole moment within the $\Xi_b^0$ baryon. Finally, the analysis of the CP-violating parameter $\phi_d$ in the decay $\Xi_b^0 \to \Xi^0 \pi^0$ is also presented. In the aftermath of disturbances of this magnitude, external support is essential to restore the system to its original operational level. We introduce a methodology to identify critical components required for quick recovery from major disturbances in supply-and-use tables (SUTs) of input-output models. Our approach utilizes the largest real eigenvalue and associated eigenvectors of the disturbance matrix. Applying this methodology to the 2012 Brazilian SUT reveals that the food industry is pivotal for swift recovery from major disturbances. Furthermore, we discovered that the resilience of this sector heavily depends on imports of animal feed from South American and North American countries, as well as financing from Germany and Switzerland. These findings are significant for policymakers and international development agencies, as they highlight the necessity of considering international economic and physical flows when formulating policies to safeguard critical industries against catastrophic disturbances. When the phenomenology of elastic scattering lacks sufficient ambition, crucial information regarding the dynamics of nucleon-nucleus and nucleus-nucleus interactions is lost. Consequently, we argue that every modern elastic scattering dataset should be accompanied by a robust theoretical analysis of the underlying phenomena. Furthermore, we highlight that recent advancements in theoretical methods and computational capabilities now permit the global analysis of all experimental data, thereby permitting stringent tests of theoretical models. This review focuses primarily on data for nuclei (or nucleons) within the laboratory energy range of roughly 10 to 1000 MeV/nucleon. Given the current state of theoretical development, our discussion centers on the phenomenological analysis of experimental results. We begin by demonstrating how the analysis of nucleon-nucleon (NN) scattering data establishes fundamental phenomenological inputs for nuclear physics and nuclear field theories. Next, we illustrate the value of these analyses by applying them to light nucleon-nucleus scattering. We then examine the analysis of data for intermediate- and heavy-target nuclei, emphasizing how these efforts refine the understanding of elastic scattering and provide valuable insights for the design of future nuclear beams. Finally, we address current challenges. First, we analyze data from nucleon-nucleus (NN) collisions at intermediate energies, where the primary challenge involves the burgeoning understanding of the role of the $\rho$-nucleon. Second, we present an overview of the analysis of nucleus-nucleus (A+A) elastic scattering data, focusing on the extensive data available for central carbon beams produced in the SPS and RHIC accelerators. In this context, we examine how the analysis of these data constrains nuclear model parameters and provides insights into nuclear reaction dynamics. We conclude by briefly outlining future directions and potential applications. Given the rapid advancements in both experimental and theoretical capabilities, we anticipate that the analysis of elastic scattering data will increasingly influence both nuclear and high-energy experimental programs. Furthermore, we foresee that the analysis of various new datasets will soon address numerous open questions concerning nucleon-nucleus and nucleus-nucleus interactions. We also outline several specific open questions and outline potential paths toward their resolution. In summary, we conclude that the analysis of elastic scattering data holds significant value and plays an essential role in advancing both the understanding and the analysis of nucleon-nucleus and nucleus-nucleus interactions. We anticipate that this perspective will gain widespread acceptance and significantly shape the future of nuclear physics research and accelerator program planning. We

is especially difficult when numerous locations are disclosed within a brief timeframe. This difficulty stems largely from the high degree of interdependence expected between these points. We introduce a privacy framework where privacy is quantified by the extent of this dependence. The model defines privacy as the maximum permissible level of mutual information between two consecutive locations. Utilizing this framework, we present multi-dimensional multihop routing and clustering methodologies that ensure the anticipated degree of privacy. Specifically, we introduce a routing protocol that steers the sequence of destinations toward one another to enhance user privacy when interacting with service providers. Additionally, we propose two clustering methods that generate location sequences with a high probability of achieving the desired privacy level. Evaluation results indicate that the routing approach boosts privacy by up to 50% without sacrificing routing efficiency, while both clustering methods meet privacy requirements while maintaining application efficiency. These methods are applicable to practical multi-dimensional environments. Furthermore, the proposed multi-dimensional multihop approach yields improvements over existing two-dimensional methods by accounting for actual geographic coordinates and application-specific requirements. Consequently, this work establishes novel principles and methodologies for privacy-preserving multihop routing and clustering in multi-dimensional settings. Extensive experiments utilizing real-world traces demonstrate that the proposed approach improves privacy across various scenarios and trace datasets compared to current state-of-the-art solutions. Furthermore, these proposals are efficient enough for deployment in practical scenarios, with estimated server processing times falling between 0.00005 and 0.055 seconds per query. Additionally, we propose a new metric for privacy evaluation in multi-dimensional contexts, which quantifies the maximum privacy provided by an algorithm or service. This newly defined privacy metric enables practitioners to select providers based on their ability to protect user privacy and helps designers set appropriate privacy levels for applications. Finally, our method is sound and effective in preserving user privacy against both membership inference and frame of reference revelation attacks, as well as frame of reference inference attacks. By measuring privacy via mutual information, this method offers a more intuitive and natural privacy metric than existing approaches in multi-dimensional scenarios. Through this research, we aim to lay a foundation for practical deployment that balances privacy and efficiency in real-world situations. The source code is available at https://github.com/locpr01.

While conventional data analysis typically treats each participant's data as an isolated unit, focusing on individual functional connectivity maps often obscures population-level findings. To address this, we introduce a functional connectivity connectivity-based likelihood maximization (FcCLBM) framework that directly models the group-level distribution of connectivity patterns, significantly enhancing statistical power and effect size estimation. Our results show that FcCLBM yields more robust and interpretable statistical outcomes, with superior and more consistent performance compared to two standard state-of-the-art methods. Our primary objective is to minimize both the energy consumption and execution time of algorithms solving these issues. We present randomized algorithms that achieve optimal performance for both naming and counting on networks of $n$ stations, with a running time of $O(n \log n)$ and an energy complexity of $O(\log n)$. Additionally, we offer algorithms with an energy complexity of $O(\log^2 n)$, which is nearly optimal, while maintaining a running time no greater than the optimal randomized algorithm. These protocols operate without preprocessing or precommunication, are fully asynchronous, and function across any speed $s \geq 1$. Our results significantly advance the state of the art, as no other randomized algorithms exist that solve naming or counting with (nearly) optimal energy complexity on single-hop beeping networks. Our solutions are also applicable to counting modulo $s$. All proposed algorithms rely on a novel randomized method for generating and detecting random numbers. Furthermore, we provide an almost linear lower bound for solving name-gathering (which requires solving naming) in terms of energy on asynchronous single-hop beeping networks, implying an almost linear energy lower bound for any method with a linear running time. This finding is nearly optimal, as we also demonstrate an algorithm with (nearly) linear energy complexity. These algorithms utilize the new randomized method for number generation, which is independent of the speed $s$. The almost linear lower bound for single-hop beeping networks follows from the existence of an upper bound. Additionally, we offer an upper bound for solving name-gathering with (nearly) linear energy on time channels using our randomized algorithm. Finally, we introduce a new algorithm for the guessing problem, a task related to solving naming on specific channels, achieving $(n-1)$-guessing with $O(\log n)$ energy. This represents an optimal energy complexity, as we also provide an energy lower bound. The result is not only nearly optimal but also significantly more efficient than the only existing upper bound. In the context of counting, it constitutes an energy breakthrough, as it allows counting any number of stations with $(n-1)$-energy using a randomized algorithm. This result is also almost linear in energy. Our algorithms run significantly faster than previous solutions, with a running time of $O(n \log n)$. This running time is optimal. Addressing the high cost of maintaining an existing annotation dataset has led many researchers to focus on cost reduction rather than cost elimination, often resulting in the reuse of annotation techniques across different medical imaging domains. This study investigates whether constraint synthesis can offer a cost-effective solution for new annotations. By training an FCN to learn the style of existing annotations and creating new constraints based on a specific medical imaging structure, we aim to reduce the time and expertise required for manual labeling while maintaining annotation quality. Our results demonstrate that this constraint-guided annotation strategy outperforms traditional bounding box methods, confirming the viability of using constraint synthesis to streamline the annotation process. Nevertheless, recent studies have demonstrated that information can still be inferred from communication data in FL, rendering such learning protocols vulnerable to communication leakage attacks (CLA). To mitigate this leakage, existing mitigation techniques typically depend on trusted third parties or secure enclaves; however, the inherent lack of trust in these enclaves limits their practicality, while maintaining a trusted party compromises system privacy. This paper introduces a novel framework for FL that enables the training of machine learning models by an untrusted server, thereby eliminating the need for a trusted party. Specifically, we introduce two online learning procedures that extend online convex optimization methods to handle linear models, enabling the learning of non-linear functions within a contextual bandit framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these proposed algorithms achieve performance comparable to that of the expert the oracle selects. As a primary application, we focus on the context of digital advertising, where a publisher selects an advertisement from an available set for each linearly modeled user. In this scenario, user engagement is unobserved, meaning clicks are not immediately visible; engagement is instead approximated by preview clicks, which are inexpensive but imperfect indicators of actual engagement. While prior research has attempted to incorporate click proxies into online learning for advertising, our work demonstrates that existing approaches fail to guarantee bounds on regret or coverage relative to an optimal expert. In contrast, we provide such guarantees using our introduced extensions of the Exp4 family. Our experimental results strongly suggest that our proposed learning procedures surpass current state-of-the-art methods. Finally, we establish that any online learning algorithm must incur a linear number of comparisons with the expert chosen by an oracle, indicating an inherent cost to learning in this setting. Our experiments, conducted in collaboration with a real publisher, show that our methods significantly outperform existing techniques. To our knowledge, this represents the first time an online learning algorithm has demonstrated superior learning from click proxies in a live advertising environment.
