However, transmitting data over the IP-based Internet introduces significant latency, which hinders real-time CPS operations. The Internet2 initiative has been driving research into a new high-performance network architecture that integrates wireless and fiber-optic technologies, enabling CPS activities while minimizing (a) end-to-end transmission delay and (b) data usage on the Internet. This paper outlines the architecture of this emerging high-performance network and introduces iCyPhy, a simulation environment designed to model CPS operations within an Internet2-like network, thereby facilitating CPS design optimization for delay-sensitive contexts. The architecture supports three primary types of CPS communication: wireless ad-hoc networks, point-to-point wireless links, and IP-connected server access via IP-over-wavelength and non-IP server access via IP-unconnected-wavelength. To represent delay-sensitive CPS operations, the model incorporates delay-critical and delay-insensitive data flows, bufferbusting flows, and data caching at access point servers and edge devices. Furthermore, the model integrates IP network functions through an IP network function call, allowing for the optimization of these functions in conjunction with CPS operations. The paper presents initial simulation results for delay-critical CPS data flows, demonstrating a performance improvement of over 2.5 times compared to standard Internet-based CPS data transmission. Additionally, the study demonstrates the potential of combining delay-critical CPS operations with IP network functions to delay-mitigate delay-insensitive data flows, achieving performance gains of over 10 times within the delay-critical CPS network environment. These findings confirm the viability of integrating CPS operations with the Internet2 high-performance network architecture. The iCyPhy model is publicly available for download at http://www.cs.psu.edu/~vkrstic/iCyPhy. Standard models regarding these SEDs in blazars remain contentious due to conflicting observations of absorption lines in quasi-stellar object (QSO) SEDs when observed through blazar SEDs. Recent studies suggest these discrepancies could be resolved if the QSO and blazar SEDs arise from mechanisms operating on vastly different scales. This work introduces a model for high-redshift blazar SEDs utilizing a core-dominated accretion flow (CDAF) around a supermassive black hole (SMBH). We demonstrate that a multi-ring structure within the CDAF naturally produces a double-humped SED with peak frequencies matching observations, alongside excess flux at high-energy gamma-rays and low-frequency radio waves. These findings align with recent measurements indicating that SMBHs in high-z star-forming galaxies possess a higher fraction of CDAFs compared to thin accretion disk (TAD) SMBHs. Consequently, we conclude that a core-dominated accretion model offers a viable explanation for the SEDs of QSOs and blazars. Additionally, utilizing the blazar SED model, we forecast that upcoming CTA observations will detect a substantial fraction of blazars emitting TEV-range radiation via hadronic interactions. We also provide evidence that a CDAF model explains the origin of very high-energy (VHE) gamma-rays from blazars, addressing a long-standing problem that has hindered the development of a robust hadronic model for QSO and blazar SEDs. We present a unified formalism applicable to various geometric configurations, specifically addressing return-point memory in ultramanetic triangular lattice spin glasses and in square lattice spin glasses composed of ferromagnetic and glassy layers. Our findings indicate that the energy landscapes of these systems are extremely rugged, displaying many metastable states with energies an $O(1)$ amount above the global minimum. Furthermore, for ultramanetic triangular lattice spin glasses, we demonstrate that the density of these metastable states exhibits a power-law scaling relative to their relaxation time, thereby confirming the persistence of this return-point memory property. In contrast, square lattice spin glasses with ferromagnetic and glassy layers exhibit more smooth landscapes; consequently, the density of metastable states decays faster than any power law with increasing system size, and these states are not glassy in nature. These results are derived from extensive Monte Carlo simulations performed both above and below the glass transition temperature. Additionally, our analysis of the density of metastable states reveals the nuanced roles played by different interaction strengths and anisotropies within triangular lattice spin glasses. Ultimately, our study enhances our comprehension of the complex energy landscapes inherent to glass and solid systems. This understanding may facilitate the rapid identification of low-energy metastable states, a capability potentially applicable to the design of new functional and intelligent materials. Furthermore, it may enable the rapid detection of return-point memory and the location of local minima within these materials. Finally, our research offers valuable insights into the energy landscapes encountered in machine learning, particularly within image and video processing tasks. The implications for these fields stem from the extensive search processes involved in determining the optimal outputs required to minimize associated loss functions. The search for these extrema can be effectively modeled by traversing an energy landscape, a process made significantly more challenging by the presence of metastable states. Consequently, our research sheds light on the complexities encountered during these extensive searches. We introduce an online strategy achieving a success probability of $\sin^2(\pi/(2N))$, which surpasses the upper limit of $\sin^2(\pi/(3N))$ associated with any optimal online joint measurement-based strategy. Furthermore, we establish an upper bound of $\cos^2(\pi/(2N))$ for such online measurement strategies, demonstrating that our proposed strategy for state discrimination meets this limit. We analyze the performance of this online approach as $N$ increases and along specific asymptotic paths, finding that it outperforms the best online unitary-based strategy by a factor of two. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between our findings and optimal collective strategies, with comparisons to existing results on distinguishing symmetric states drawn. Finally, we extend our primary result to the discrimination of generic pure states, achieving a success probability of $\sin^2(3\theta\pi/(2N))$, where $\theta$ represents the known a priori knowledge regarding the number of copies per register. These findings are compared to current optimal joint and local discrimination bounds. Furthermore, we identify a correspondence between discriminating symmetric states and discriminating specific types of pure states, allowing us to derive a new upper bound of $\sin^2(\theta\pi/(2N-1))$ for the latter problem, which asymptotically approaches one-half. This bound is achieved when the initial state of the pure system is either pure or mixed with eigenvalues $\{1-\epsilon, \epsilon, \epsilon, \epsilon\}$. Our bound remains valid regardless of the dimension of the pure system, remaining independent of the Hilbert space dimension. Additionally, we identify a family of local strategies that attain this bound. These insights into generic pure states may aid in understanding the behavior of better local (online) strategies for generic symmetric states as $N \to \infty$. It remains an open question whether an optimal local (online) strategy for generic symmetric states can achieve an asymptotic success probability greater than one-half. More broadly, we believe these insights into optimal local strategies for pure states may prove valuable in investigating discrimination tasks. Furthermore, we identify a class of pure states whose discrimination aligns with that of symmetric states, a class that includes states already studied in the literature. Our work includes an analysis of the performance of the online strategy relative to increasing the dimension of the pure state space, as well as the asymptotic behavior of this strategy.

measuring the travel times of acoustic waves propagating radially in the Sun's interior offers insights into regional sound-speed variations caused by solar activity. Determining these travel times relies on identifying wave-front arrivals within acoustic centrals (Pm modes), which are exceptionally sharp signals generated when moving sound-speed gradients refract sound waves into the solar center. **Aims.** This study presents a novel local helioseismic analysis of solar active regions using envelope detection and autocorrelation methods to calculate travel times of acoustic waves from active regions to the Sun's center, alongside an investigation into the precise location of the apparent source of Pm waves. **Methods.** Employing data from the space-based Ground-based Adaptive Telescope for Observing solar Acoustic resonances (GATO), we identified apparent sources of Pm waves and computed travel times from these sources to the solar center for one active region observed at the disk center and another observed at a disk latitude of 48 degrees. **Results.** We determined that Pm wave sources originate from formally infinite distances but are effectively located at the nearby active region. Encouragingly, we found that enclosing these Pm sources within a small zone and averaging travel times within that zone significantly reduces scatter while maintaining accuracy relative to predictions derived from active-region sound speeds. Additionally, applying a fast-local-convex-tomography inversion to the measured travel times yielded sound-speed profiles consistent with solar-model predictions. **Conclusions.** By averaging travel times from Pm wave sources to the solar interior, envelope detection combined with autocorrelation provides accurate data crucial for future investigations into solar-sound-speed variations induced by magnetic fields. This approach holds particular promise for tomographic analyses in the outer 30,000 km of the Sun's interior. **Paper 2.** This is Paper 1 of 2; Paper 2: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1190207. , and International Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) Collaborations have all reported a common signal characteristic of a stochastic GW background within the PTA frequency band. However, contrary to the $\lambda^{-1/2}$ slope anticipated from cosmological models, the amplitude of these reported signals rises as the harmonic frequency decreases. This study employs a Power Spectrum Maximum Likelihood Estimator to reanalyze the combined data from all 682 pulsars in the NANOGrav 13-year dataset, successfully reproducing the standard NANOGrav fit results. Furthermore, we test the signal against seven distinct functional forms to identify the most probable model and assess its significance. Our primary finding indicates that, when excluding an unphysical exponential form, a power-law model with a spectral index of $ \lambda=-2/3$ best aligns with the data alongside an offset, with statistical support for this specific power law. Among the power-law models tested ($\lambda=-2/3, -1/2, 0, 1/2, 1$), the model with an index of $\lambda=-2/3$ exhibits the strongest correlation ($\rho=0.998$) with the full NANOGrav fit, which is constrained to a combination of this power law and an offset. We hypothesize that this signal may originate from a cosmological phase transition during the QCD transition in the early universe. Leveraging the parametric flexibility of the $-2/3$ power law, we constrain the gravitational wave background (GWB) energy density ratio to $(\Omega_{GW}/\rho_{c})_{max}^{2/3}=1.4-12.2(68\%~{\rm C.L.})\times 10^{-10}$ and the universe's baryonic density to $0.197-0.222(68\%~{\rm C.L.})$, the latter being lower than typical $\Lambda$CDM estimates. Consequently, our analysis suggests that PTA signals are more likely linked to QCD phase transitions than to supermassive binary systems. Nevertheless, if the signal stems from supermassive binary evolution, our constraints suggest the gravitational wave spectrum would have declined over time, moving away from $f^{-2}$ behavior toward $f^{-1}$. In either scenario, the GW spectrum is constrained to lie below the LISA and DECIGO sensitivity curves while remaining within the sensitivity range

We introduce a novel non-interactive method grounded in Bayesian unsupervised domain adaptation, leveraging weakly supervised cross-entropy minimization without requiring domain alignment or image transformation. Specifically, our approach utilizes image patches, operating under the assumption that certain patches from one domain closely resemble those from another, despite overall domain disparities. Experimental results demonstrate that our technique surpasses state-of-the-art benchmarks on the MNIST, MNIST2MNIST, MNIST+MNIST2MNIST, and Fei4Meds datasets. This method relies on neural network parameter optimization utilizing data augmented by a policy gradient term. Core to our approach is the concept of implicit models, which are learned directly within the operational state space without the need to model intermediate spaces like action or state vectors. These implicit models function by representing the system dynamics as the solution to an implicit equation that balances an energy term against a cross-entropy term. By resolving this equation, we derive a DAE-solver-based feedback policy. Using gradient-based parameter updates, we enhance this policy to achieve the control objectives. To ensure training stability, modifications to the implicit model are calculated based on the spectral radius of the Jacobian of the DAE residual, ensuring the system remains in the "basin of attraction" of its neural network definition. We demonstrate that stochastic gradient descent can be applied to learn the parameters of the neural network implicit model, effectively minimizing the discrepancy between the learned model and the true dynamical system. Our findings indicate that it is feasible to learn implicit models and their corresponding DAE-solvers/policy gradients from sparse and partially observed data, even when dealing with non-conservative dynamics. Furthermore, we show that the proposed algorithm can be viewed as a reinforcement learning method. Consequently, we developed this novel deep learning technique for learning-based control, showing its high efficiency in solving high-dimensional problems. We validated the results through simulations of high-dimensional robotic systems, including the Bouncing Ball Problem, the Double Pendulum, and the Urn Problem. Additionally, we applied our method to a real-world drone, conducting both simulated and physical experiments to confirm its effectiveness. Finally, we compared our approach with other learning-based control techniques found in the literature. Our method, which learns implicit models representing dynamical systems, successfully acquires the underlying model from sparse and noisy data and utilizes it to execute control tasks, even when the observation process is completely unknown. Within Toda theories, these fields are associated with the matrices defining a $l$-tuple of framed sl$_n$- representations of a finitely generated group $\Xi$. The matrices corresponding to $\Xi$ are collected in a representation variety $\mathcal{X}(\Xi, \mathbb{C}^*/\pm 1, \rho)$. This work demonstrates that the curvature of the affine connection on $\mathcal{X}(\Xi, \mathbb{C}^*/\pm 1, \rho)$ arises from a collection of conformal field theories defined on a Riemann surface of genus zero featuring four punctures. Specifically, the target matrices of the associated Toda fields correspond to the Pochhammer amplitude of the KZ connection, thereby linking the geometry of the representation variety with the physics of the Toda conformal field theory. Consequently, the matrices of the resulting Pochhammer representation can be viewed as conformal field theory interpretations of the monodromy of the KZ connection within the four-punctured sphere vertex operator algebra. Ultimately, this study seeks to bridge the algebraic geometry of the representation variety with the physical framework of Toda conformal field theory. This study examines the implications of utilizing non-linear factor models for mortality forecasting. Utilizing non-linear factors allows for a more comprehensive capture of mortality dynamics, particularly for defining interactions among demographic characteristics such as age, sex, and cause of death. Addressing the growing challenge of disinformation, this research explores whether large-scale social media platforms can leverage their substantial resources to mitigate misinformation and safeguard democracy. Specifically, it presents a framework for designing and implementing data-driven interventions using high-volume data from Facebook's ad and content moderation teams. By applying this approach to U.S. political misinformation, the study demonstrates that targeted, data-driven advertising can effectively reduce the spread of disinformation across the Facebook platform. Finally, we discuss the challenges and policy considerations inherent in designing and executing such large-scale, data-driven efforts. To support future interventions, we release a highly granular dataset comprising Facebook's actions regarding political misinformation in the U.S. during 2017 and 2018, along with a comprehensive analysis of the associated allegations. This data reveals nuanced patterns in Facebook's intervention approach and offers a valuable resource for researchers and policymakers. This work is presented in the INSEAD Executive Program on Data-Driven Interventions for Social Good, a three-day initiative hosted in Paris in September 2019. Previously, these matrix's eigenvalues and eigenvectors were defined in terms of the geometry of both the wavefront and the target. In this study, we establish analogous definitions for scattering media where the surface properties vary randomly and remain independent of the incident wavefront. Our key findings demonstrate that in such media, the eigenvalues depend exclusively on the target volume, while the eigenvectors are determined solely by the medium's surface properties, which are independent of the incoming wave. This insight suggests a method to characterize random media based on the structure of the deposition matrix. Furthermore, we model statistically homogeneous random media by averaging over all possible random realizations to derive "resulting" eigenvalues and eigenvectors. The resulting dominant eigenvalue aligns with the Bragg scattering wavelength, which is visible on the surface of diffuse samples, while the dominant eigenvector represents the spatial structure of the eigenmode associated with the maximum scattering probability. Consequently, our analysis predicts the likelihood of multiple eigenmodes being excited within the target volume. Finally, we apply these findings to a simulation model that accounts for the scattering and multiple scattering of light within biological tissue. Additionally, we suggest that the multiplicative model, which has previously modeled coherent diffusion of energy in such tissues, serves as an ideal representation of the target field linked to the leading eigenvalue and eigenvector. These results offer valuable analytical and practical applications. By characterizing random media via the deposition matrix, new eigenvalue-based diagnostics can be developed to guide wave propagation. For biological tissue, which acts as a strongly random medium, analysis allows for the prediction and optimization of wave propagation and the resulting absorbed energy. Specifically, this enables insights into how wavefront shaping can enhance the excitation of multiple eigenmodes within the tissue. Ultimately, these capabilities can significantly improve optical diagnostics and therapeutic interventions. While the straightforward approach of removing entire units is computationally efficient, advanced methods that prune individual connections offer greater flexibility. However, this increased flexibility often depends on the internal activation values of pruned units, creating a situation where pruning a single unit could trigger the unexpected pruning of multiple others. To address this, we introduce an algorithm that manages these interdependencies and mitigates the issue ofpruning units with zero input or output weights, which would otherwise be unprunable. Testing this algorithm on the standard pruning task—reducing a ResNet-56 by 20% of its parameters while maintaining accuracy on MNIST—revealed that incorporating ZeroPadding boosted performance, while ZeroFilling had no such benefit. Furthermore, our analysis of various pruning variants indicates that the advantages of Advanced Pruning are especially pronounced in networks utilizing ZeroFilling. By enhancing core Advanced Pruning algorithms, this work facilitates a more granular and thorough search for optimal solutions within the hyperparameter search space. Ultimately, our core contribution enables a more flexible methodology for applying Advanced Pruning, opening new avenues for future research. Millions and Powerball draw more participants, thereby raising the chance of multiple winners sharing the pot. Consequently, as the probability of at least one non-lucky holder rises, jackpot growth may contribute to market instability. This study examines the influence of repeated play on these shared gains. By integrating game-theoretic models of player behavior with empirical data from US lottery transactions, we analyze how the "hot hand" fallacy—believing that recent wins increase future winning odds—drives the demand for specific tickets. Our findings indicate that while repeated play can reduce the likelihood of shared jackpots by more than 50%, this effect diminishes rapidly, reaching near zero within four to five rounds. We conclude that the instability associated with large jackpots is primarily driven by the "herd behavior" of repeated players. Furthermore, our model offers a quantitative basis for understanding the correlation between jackpot size and total lottery revenue. By assessing the total value of all tickets, our methodology aids regulators in monitoring market instability and supports designers in crafting less volatile lottery games..

Within the $1/Q$ expansion framework for harmonic-oscillator-confining Coulomb systems, we demonstrate that the large-charge expansion series in powers of $1/Q$ converges rapidly toward the exact many-body ground-state energy. Our findings indicate that the leading-order Harman-Kogan large-charge expansion accurately predicts the specific heat, correlation length, charge density, electric field, electron density, and entropy of the many-body system up to higher-order corrections. Leveraging scaling arguments alongside recent exact solutions to the single-particle problem in $1/4$ spatial dimensions, we demonstrate that the leading-order approximation yields entirely analytical and dimension-independent results. Furthermore, we examine the single-electron limit of the large-charge expansion, revealing that the leading-order Harman-Kogan result replicates the exact mean-field energy within the same dimensionally independent form. Additionally, we introduce a generalized large-charge expansion framework capable of generating analytical, dimensionally independent leading-order Harman-Kogan-like results for arbitrary values of the confinement-coulomb ratio $\eta=Q/R$. The implications of these dimensionally and single-parameter dependent analytical results are discussed in the context of potential experimental applications in the electronic and excitonic large-charge regime. Finally, we explore the physical mechanisms behind the exceptional accuracy of the leading-order expansion and rigorously analyze the validity and convergence of this series against the exact many-body result. We demonstrate that for parameter regimes where many-body effects are strong, the many-particle problem can be effectively mapped onto the single-particle problem via a shift in the single-particle potential's minimum. Conversely, we show that when many-body effects are weak, specifically near the electron exciton transition point, the large-charge expansion converges slowly, signaling a possible critical point within the phase diagram at this specific transition. This slow convergence is rigorously proven by mapping the higher-order corrections of the large-charge expansion onto the Reshetikhin diagram of weakly interacting bosons. Our results establish the new paradigm that the specific heat of quantum matter exhibits universal single-particle scaling near a critical point in its phase diagram, a concept originally proposed by Wilson and Fisher in critical phenomena and subsequently observed in many-body systems far from criticality in the single-electron limit. This critical specific heat near the electron exciton transition point within the large-charge expansion regime represents a direct experimental verification of the expansion's validity

By comparing our results against recent experimental data, TG-simulation (using the Luttinger liquid approximation), and theoretical proposals for low-density fermionic systems, we find that the polaron exhibits 2D Fermi-liquid characteristics at low densities, with both the quasiparticle residue and the polaron energy within the sea of a Fermi gas showing linear scaling relative to the scattering length. As interactions intensify, strong coupling and non-Fermi liquid effects become more pronounced, ultimately leading to the 2D BCS BEC regime, where polaron excitations within the Fermi sea transform into magnons associated with the emergence of Luttinger liquids. These findings offer compelling candidates for exploration in advanced \textit{degenerate} $^6$Li or $^{40}$K experiments. Furthermore, our results suggest that energy shifts in the low-energy spectrum of real spinor Bose gases, where spinor components interact via $s$-wave p-wave channels utilizing Pauli blocking, may similarly stem from non-Fermi liquid effects. This underscores the potential for deeper understanding and more precise measurements of energy spectra using state-of-the-art Bose-Einstein condensate experiments, which possess the capability to access the unitary limit. Finally, the DiagMC method utilized here holds promise for future applications in understanding polarons in other complex and emergent systems, such as Fermi liquids, Wigner crystals, and topological insulators. This paper examines two variants of the Strauss process: $\mathcal{P}_1$, which shares the same inhomogeneous intensity function as the Strauss process but employs a non-Poisson background, and $\mathcal{P}_2$, which utilizes a Poisson background but deviates from the Strauss density definition. We compare the performance of these two processes. First, we control the total number of points by culling $\mathcal{P}_1$ and $\mathcal{P}_2$ samples to match their expected cardinalities. Next, we thicken both modified processes to a common interaction radius $\rho$. We demonstrate that as $\rho$ increases, the data from $\mathcal{P}_1$ converges to a hard-core process, whereas $\mathcal{P}_2$ converges to a different point process. Consequently, in terms of predicted richness, $\mathcal{P}_1$ behaves like a hard-core process, while $\mathcal{P}_2$ exhibits the richer structure characteristic of a Strauss process. We attribute this discrepancy to the method used to equate the expected cardinalities of $\mathcal{P}_1$ and $\mathcal{P}_2$. Finally, we illustrate this difference using real data. The paper begins with an introduction, followed by a review of the literature. We then present a literature review. Subsequently, we introduce $\mathcal{P}_1$ and $\mathcal{P}_2$ via their characteristic functions, define their densities, and compare their properties, differences, and applications. Finally, we demonstrate the distinction between $\mathcal{P}_1$ and $\mathcal{P}_2$ through numerical simulations, showing how $\mathcal{P}_1$ converges to a hard-core process as $\rho$ increases, while $\mathcal{P}_2$ approaches a Strauss process. We also analyze whether $\mathcal{P}_1$ and $\mathcal{P}_2$ can model identical datasets, finding that for $\mathcal{P}_1$, increasing $\rho$ reduces predicted richness, a behavior not observed in $\mathcal{P}_2$. We provide a numerical example comparing the richness of $\mathcal{P}_1$ and $\mathcal{P}_2$ for a specific data set.

This study investigates the implications of such a minimum domain on wave function normalization within the framework of GUP, demonstrating how to construct properly normalized Wigner functions for free particles and harmonic oscillators. A primary application of the Wigner function lies in defining phase space regions to quantify signal detectability. We show that the GUP modifies the minimum domain size in phase space, quantifying this change relative to the minimum length scale, which can be linked to the Planck mass. Furthermore, by treating photon mass as a function of energy in the Wigner distribution, we observe that both the minimum domain and the Wigner function's decay into the quantum Tsallis region are influenced by quantum and gravitational effects, contingent upon the magnitude of the GUP deformation parameter. These findings may assist in developing a more comprehensive model of photon detection, incorporating both quantum and gravitational influences. Additionally, we examine the impact of GUP on entropy, specifically the von Neumann entropy derived from the Wigner function, comparing it with the linear entropy to define the transition to the thermal region and the thermalization process for GUP-deformed Wigner distributions. The paper concludes that quantum and gravitational effects must be considered when investigating microscopic systems approaching the Planck mass scale. This conclusion is supported by an investigation of the blackbody spectrum using GUP-deformed phase space regions, which predicts a shift in the spectral density peak toward higher temperatures determined by the GUP parameter. Ultimately, we propose an experimental framework grounded in blackbody radiation to constrain the GUP deformation parameter. Finally, we highlight current limitations in determining this parameter and advocate for future research aimed at establishing more sensitive methods to measure it. These findings may also extend to modeling classical wave packets with minimum domains, such as those generated by laser-cooled atoms. Overall, this work seeks to bridge the gap between high-energy and low-energy physics by creating a unified approach to microscopic phenomena that simultaneously accounts for quantum and gravitational effects. In settings such as hospitals, multitasking is inherent, necessitating that service units handle multiple tasks within a single service period. This study addresses the issue of energy-efficient and timely multitasking scheduling through a two-stage approach. Initially, we convert the original scheduling challenge into an activity completion period (ACP) prediction problem, which is solved using both traditional machine learning (ML) models and deep learning (DL) frameworks to minimize prediction errors. In the second stage, we develop a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) algorithm utilizing precast ACP data, optimizing for both operational costs and energy consumption. The proposed method, termed ML/DRL, is contrasted with two DRL baselines that employ different cost functions and a network scheduling baseline. Extensive simulations on a real-world hospital dataset demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses all benchmarks. Additionally, results indicate that DL and DRL models are robust to variations in input features, a critical advantage in real-world environments where input features are often incomplete or inaccurate. Finally, our extensive experiments reveal that incorporating energy costs into the objective function substantially improves scheduling efficiency. These findings suggest that accounting for energy consumption is particularly advantageous in large-scale and resource-constrained operations. This discrepancy arises from the dynamic deformation of soft surfaces under actuator forces and gravity, which alters the contact interactions between legs and the terrain. This study investigates the effectiveness of control policies designed to transfer locomotion skills between rigid and soft environments. Specifically, we evaluate two policies: one trained exclusively on a rigid terrain and another trained directly on a soft terrain. Our findings indicate that policies trained on soft terrain generalize effectively to other soft environments with varying material parameters. Each potential barrier is modeled as having a linear slope and is defined by a single parameter. To address this multi-channel scattering system, we utilize molecular orbitals formed from the product of one-dimensional even and odd parities of the wave functions within each segment. This formulation yields two sets of recursive matrix elements—one for each parity—that enable the calculation of any system parameter given the other. This sensitivity offers a viable method for modulating conductance in mesoscopic two-dimensional field effect transistors. Similar to non-interactive searches, non-interactive pure strategies are optimal for interactive ones, but the converse does not hold. We define the interaction parameter, which measures the expected number of label queries in an optimal interactive search. This parameter scales as a polynomial of degree no greater than 2, relying on graph parameters that characterize the difficulty of distinguishing target labels. As a primary application, we examine the optimal interactive search for distinguishing labels assigned to two sets of distinct trees. The complexity of this scenario is governed by either the relative depth difference or the size disparity between the two tree sets. Furthermore, we explore the interplay between interaction and computational cost. Specifically, we demonstrate that searches which are nearly optimal both computation-wise and interaction-wise can be constructed in polynomial time, provided the graph is a pair of distinct trees. These findings significantly broaden the scope of feasible interactive searches. Additionally, our results establish that optimal interactive searches for complete graphs and uniform label assignments can be computed in constant and linear time, respectively. Finally, we examine the relationship between interactive and quasi-interactive pure strategies, showing that the latter can efficiently emulate the former. This efficiency is assessed by the relative difference in the number of queries required. Consequently, any problem solvable in quasi-interactive time can be solved interactively in quadratic time, regardless of the parameters, confirming the practicality of such searches. Furthermore, this approach enables a polynomial speedup for searches where a quasi-optimal (quasi-computable) strategy exists. Conceptually, this work represents the initial step toward implementing quasi-computable strategies. Alignments represent a cutting-edge method for identifying, locating, and measuring deviations in process executions (traces) relative to reference process models. However, alignments typically require complete process executions that span from start to finish, or at least prefixes of such executions. This paper introduces infix/postfix alignments, representing a novel approach to deviation analysis for incomplete trace fragments found within ongoing process executions. Specifically, we propose methods to generate these alignments and calculate the costs they reveal, utilizing subsequence-based deviation detection. Additionally, this paper provides a formal definition of alignment-derived deviations, outlines two approaches for inferring goal achievement from partial trace fragments, and analyzes the computational complexity associated with alignments in this context. The behavior of fragments is modeled using prefix Petri nets, which are demonstrated to be sufficiently expressive for most practical applications involving ongoing process executions. An experimental section illustrates how deviations inferred from fragment postices can effectively identify and position missing variations compared to full alignments, with experiments also reporting performance metrics. Experimental inferences were conducted on realistic fragment postices extracted from event logs of a煤矿 (coal mine) management system. Furthermore, experiments analyzed the performance impact of infix alignments on overall alignment-guided deviation analysis, demonstrating that they are nearly as efficient as traditional postfix alignments. Finally, the event logs used in these experiments are available for download for further reproducibility. The remaining sections of the paper are structured as follows: Section 2 presents necessary definitions, while Section 3 defines alignments for identifying, reporting, and measuring deviations in fragmented trace variations. Section 4 details in- and postfix alignment guidance for deviation analysis. Section 5 presents the comparative evaluation, and Section 6 concludes and identifies directions for future research. Additionally, an ongoing implementation utilizing marked graph nets as prefix structures for trace fragments is discussed in Section 6, where it is shown that infix alignments perform well for goal detection in fragmental executions. While empirical models are frequently utilized due to their straightforward parameterization, they often fail to capture proper radio behavior in specific scenarios. This study introduces a complementary empirical approach specifically designed to address pathloss at near-field distances, typically within 50 meters of the base station. The proposed model characterizes the slope of the pathloss increase as a function of distance, alongside a corresponding offset, relative to the 3GPP small-cell baseline. These parameters are derived from the correlation with the base station's height above ground. To validate this model, measurements were taken inside urban buildings. The results indicate that, in the near field, building height is the dominant factor influencing pathloss, even when the distance from the base station is kept constant. Consequently, the model demonstrates high effectiveness in variable urban settings. Furthermore, this model can be integrated into existing macro-cell empirical models to create generalized models applicable to both macro and small cells. The combined model achieves higher accuracy than traditional macro-cell models, showing at least a 10 dB improvement in mean model error. Additionally, the model exhibits robustness in predicting pathloss at distances beyond the measurement range. All underlying assumptions have been confirmed, and the model's effectiveness has been verified. Based on the model's simplicity and its superior accuracy, it is well-suited for cost-effective radio propagation planning in cellular networks. A MATLAB implementation is provided in the appendix. The model's applicability to millimeter-wave frequencies is under consideration. Ultimately, the model's effectiveness is comparable to full-wave simulation methods. It is expected that this research will contribute to reduced time and costs in cellular network planning. The authors declare no conflicts of interest. However, the specific values of their non-linear rheological parameters, such as yield stress and post-yield viscosity, remain largely undefined, limiting an intuitive understanding of their micro-macro connections. This study addresses this gap by investigating the rheology of dense, weakly interacting, short-range potential soft polymer-bead gels through a systematic analysis of particle size, confinement, and contactability. Crucially, the observed trends in yield stress and post-yield viscosity align with predictions from Yield Stress models, demonstrating high sensitivity to particle size even after accounting for zero-shear viscosity. In contrast, for non-soft particles, the BYOS model fails to predict the sensitivity of rheological properties to contactability, a factor that significantly influences soft particle gels. These findings offer fundamental insights into establishing a link between the contact network and macro-scale rheology to advance the rational design of new materials. Additionally, the study reveals that standard microrheology techniques are frequently inapplicable to samples exhibiting non-linear rheological behavior. Finally, the authors emphasize that soft rheometry offers distinct advantages over other characterization methods for understanding soft granular gels. Consequently, they cannot describe nonequilibrium cold atomic systems. Instead, we assert that these processes are best modeled using an Einstein-Hopf equation, which reduces to a modified Darcy equation only at equilibrium. Furthermore, this approach enables the characterization of nonequilibrium cold atomic systems through a nonequilibrium temperature (NETD) defined as $T_{NE} = Q/D$, where $Q$ represents the amplitude of atomic position fluctuations and $D$ is the effective dimensionless diffusion coefficient. We establish that $D$ is universal, generally exceeding unity, and can be measured experimentally. Additionally, we show that $T_{NE}$ is typically lower than the center-of-mass temperature $T_c$ and can be estimated via cold atom scattering experiments. Finally, we argue that $T_{NE}$ may also apply to other scenarios involving atomic systems with short-range interactions, offering a potential explanation for the previously observed paradox of atomic expansion without external heating. This framework may also clarify the long-standing discrepancy between the heat capacity predicted by the Sackur-Tetrode equation and that derived from the Einstein-Solovov equation for liquid helium. Furthermore, we have successfully replicated key experimental findings regarding the NETD and $T_{NE}$ using a specific set of simulated atomic systems. Finally, we provide a general formula and a quick test to distinguish between simulations and experiments governed by the Einstein-Hopf equation and those that are not. Consequently, fluid exothermic reactions combined with radiation cause lasers to dissipate energy into an expanding spherical cavity within the heated zone, rather than creating a continuous heat wave path from the entry to the exit surface as seen in conductive solids. Furthermore, laser-fluid interactions generate further heating via reactions such as H₂ production or CO₂ consumption, and laser absorption triggers photolysis, all of which significantly alter the absorption length and threshold fluence. These findings explain experimental results, including an absorption length of 2.1 mm, and offer new insights for applying high-energy lasers to fluid-based energy storage and micro-reaction engineering. Additionally, these mechanisms explain the self-healing property of spatially inhomogeneous beams in turbulent turbulent convective atmospheres. Leveraging these insights, we simulated high-intensity CO₂ laser propagation in sugar-water droplets and generated molasses from ahong droplets. Based on these simulations, we successfully focused a 10 kW laser onto ahong droplets to produce ahong syrup. This paper introduces DesignEffect, a model that classifies forum threads into three categories: software design, other, and uncertain. DesignEffect achieves an F1 score of 76.5%, outperforming the previous best model (MultiLabelBOW, +6.7 points) by leveraging three novel single-text features and incorporating bicultural software forum data. Additionally, we present an algorithm to extract relevant discussions specifically for a target class. When applied to the Java framework Android with 95% confidence, DesignEffect surpasses the prior state-of-the-art algorithm for design identification (JADE), offering greater precision and a higher recall of useful recommendations. These advantages facilitate the creation of a library of Java classes annotated with discussions about their usage in software design. The source code for DesignEffect is publicly available to support its integration into existing systems or to develop new applications using this class library. Specifically, we demonstrate its utility in building automated documentation from existing project artifacts. We anticipate DesignEffect will continue to enhance the software design identification performance in this documentation project and other related applications. Our Java model achieves an F1 score of 75.0, while the Python model scores 74.3. We conducted an manual analysis of misclassified instances, which revealed an average F1 score of 78.3 for model-annotated instances reviewed by three experts. This increase in accuracy is relevant for future implementations of DesignEffect. To ensure reproducibility, all raw data and Java code for this study are openly accessible. The core contribution remains the development and validation of DesignEffect itself. This work utilizes data from StackOverflow, a platform where developers discuss various software development topics. We analyzed approximately 1.05 million English comments from Android and Java projects to train the model. Our primary contribution is the design and execution of a human validation study on misclassified cases, which established a baseline performance level. Our code for this research is available publicly. The study demonstrates that the quality of misclassified instances could be improved with a sufficient training set of existing examples. English to Romanian frequently produce ungrammatical outputs due to issues like word order errors and omitted or added articles/prepositions, which significantly hinder readability. To address this, we propose a two-stage solution utilizing a Markov Model (MM) to refine NMT predictions. Specifically, the MM is trained on high-quality parallel monolingual data from both English and Romanian. We explore two strategies for integrating this model: either directly post-editing NMT outputs or leveraging the model to train and fine-tune the original NMT system. Experimental results on the WMT'19 task demonstrate marked improvements over the baseline system in both scenarios. Notably, when leveraging the MM to fine-tune the NMT system, our approach achieves a 1.12 points gain over the raw Transformer baseline, reaching a Comet score of 70.85. Even in the post-editing framework, there is a substantial improvement compared to using NMT predictions without modification. These findings confirm that incorporating a language model fine-tuned on Romanian data within a two-stage Markov Model framework significantly enhances NMT performance. Furthermore, experiments on multiple language pairs indicate that this proposed method is effective across various languages. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first study to apply Markov Models for NMT improvement using Romanian as a target language. Finally, the post-editing results suggest promising future directions for developing automated post-editing tools for Romanian translation. ilarity-based clustering: the definition and properties of clustering algorithms, the structure of the domain under clustering, and the relationship between these clustering concepts and information-theoretic metrics. The study establishes an information-theoretic framework for clustering, state-space clustering (SSC), and utilizes SSC to evaluate the similarity of clustering algorithms. We demonstrate that SSC can represent a broad category of clustering methods operating on finite sets or finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces. For algorithms representable by a single SSC, we prove that identical clustering results are equivalent to satisfying a specific set of inequalities within the derived cross-symmetrized dissimilarity matrix. Furthermore, for clustering algorithms defined by multiple SSCs, we introduce the concept of equivalent regions to identify where differing algorithms agree and where they disagree. Additionally, we derive the most general SSC capable of representing any clustering algorithm defined on a finite set or finite-dimensional Euclidean space. Finally, we develop a novel, fast, and robust algorithm to determine the most general SSC for a specific clustering algorithm and dataset, facilitating comparisons between different methods. This approach is particularly valuable for identifying regions in high-dimensional parameter spaces where distinct clustering algorithms yield equivalent results. These insights are applied to the analysis of the optimal number of clusters in both simulated and real-world datasets. Furthermore, SSC enables the derivation of theoretical bounds on the expected intersection size of cluster sets across different algorithms and data realizations, illustrating these bounds using various methods on both simulated and real data. The efficacy of this approach in enhancing clustering understanding is highlighted through its application to well-known datasets, including the old faithfull, iris, and leukaemia datasets, as well as a new dataset involving children with Down's syndrome. Additionally, extensive simulations confirm that carefully selected SSCs can distinguish between clustering algorithms based on their fundamental properties and theoretical considerations. Ultimately, these findings support the development and selection of appropriate clustering algorithms for specific datasets or applications. To accommodate diverse data types and structures, we also explore techniques for transforming data into representations where clustering becomes more meaningful. Furthermore, we validate the utility of SSC in supervised learning contexts, showing that many clustering algorithms can be effectively learned using simple linear classifiers applied to data projected via local principal component analysis, where data points are represented by their principal components at each location. This approach, combined with carefully chosen SSCs, can differentiate between algorithms like K-means, spectral clustering, and various density-based methods. Consequently, substantial supervision is required only to identify the appropriate SSC and the optimal dimension reduction. Consequently, these findings may facilitate significant advancements in scalable and robust clustering

Nevertheless, in turbulent jets, these vortices appear to follow a inverse cascade where their characteristic size grows over time before eventually reaching a different scale. This study investigates whether jet turbulence exhibits characteristics similar to geostrophic turbulence subjected to a conserved potential vorticity constraint imposed by an initial vortex. Utilizing a Lagrangian-decomposition numerical method specifically designed to maintain conserved potential vorticity, we simulate the transient evolution of this system. Our findings indicate that both the jet's characteristic vortices and the geostrophic vortices generated by conserved potential vorticity increase in size at identical rates during the transient phase. This parallel expansion is also observed in the scales defined by enstrophy and kinetic energy. However, when two geostrophic vortices of varying sizes interact, their expansion rates diverge. We demonstrate that this discrepancy arises from ageostrophic motions, which are more pronounced in the smaller vortex. Given that enstrophy is dominated by small-scale vortices, this sensitivity to ageostrophic motions results in a distinct physical interpretation of the transient inhomogeneous geostrophic phase. Unlike the classical transient interpreted as geostrophic adjustment, this phase represents the physics of geostrophic vortices and their associated ageostrophic motions. Furthermore, the convergence between the enstrophy scale of the jet and the geostrophic vortex scale suggests a physical mechanism explaining why these distinct vortices expand at the same rate during the transient phase of a jet. This mechanism operates within a physics analogous to geostrophic turbulence, thereby linking the physics of jets to the concept of the initial geostrophic vortex. Consequently, the transient phase in both jets and geostrophic vortices is interpreted as the physical manifestation of initial geostrophic vorticity. Consequently, the characteristics of geostrophic vortices in the transient jet phase are identified as the primary source of the observed self-similarity in the early stages of a jet. Moreover, the convergence between the enstrophy scale and the geostrophic vortex scale explains the linear scaling of the scaling law during the same transient phase. Finally, we show that the classical scaling law is only briefly recovered in the late transient phase, indicating that the geostrophic vortices have nearly reached their final size. The primary objective is to analyze how electrical modulation influences these thermodynamic properties, with findings compared against those of conventional two-dimensional electron gases (2DEG). The research examines graphone crystals, the thermodynamics of doped graphene, and doped graphone. Numerical simulations reveal that the thermodynamic potential of a 2DEG in electrical modulation varies cyclically with a work cycle, indicating that non-equilibrium thermodynamic states can be achieved by doping monolayer graphene with electrical modulation. This effect is more pronounced in graphone crystals than in 2DEG. The potential of doped graphene outside modulation periods does not exhibit cyclic behavior, as these regions can be treated as equilibrium states possessing specific thermodynamic properties. The thermodynamic potential of doped graphene within the magnetic field achieves local extrema when the Fermi level aligns with Dirac points in the Landau level (LL) structure, a state that can also be induced by electrical modulation. For graphone, the thermodynamic potential reaches local extrema when the LL centers align with Dirac points in graphene. The impact of the electric field on thermodynamic parameters is more significant in graphene than in 2DEG. Regarding 2DEG in electrical modulation with doping, the thermodynamic potential remains cyclically periodic despite the presence of charge carriers, as the dopant particles do not contribute to the thermodynamic potential and remain stationary. These findings indicate that electrical modulation offers a means to control various thermodynamic parameters in monolayer graphene. Additionally, the capacity to reach non-equilibrium thermodynamic states in electrical modulation within the framework of Landau-Fermi statistics suggests that electrical modulation can serve as an engine to execute thermodynamic cycles, thereby performing work. The ability to manipulate thermodynamic parameters in graphene, potentially for use as a working substance in this cycle, distinguishes this approach from standard thermodynamic cycle frameworks. Furthermore, the ability to utilize graphone thermodynamic parameters distinguishes this method from typical engine components. Consequently, this research paves the way for developing new graphene-based thermodynamic devices. The use of graphene as a thermodynamic material, where non-equilibrium thermodynamic states act as the working substance, represents a novel concept. The proposed work may find applications in designing new graphene-based thermodynamic devices. The developed theory and numerical simulations hold the promise of expanding to more complex graphene structures, such as graphene transistors. To address this, we employed the Arecibo 305-m telescope to conduct targeted searches for such coherent radio emissions from four known M-dwarf active stars: UV Ceti, AD Leticiae, TV Eridani, and UV Lemerquiere. **I. INTRODUCTION**  
Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning technique designed to train models across distributed data without the requirement of centralized access. By leveraging client-side data availability, FL enables training speedups compared to centralized methods, while preserving data privacy by keeping information localized. However, accessing client-side data is not always feasible, and ensuring security through mere isolation is insufficient; thus, FL is particularly suited for heterogeneous data environments.

The foundational assumption underlying most existing FL research is access to homogeneous communication links between the server and every client. Furthermore, the computational and communication costs associated with training are frequently treated as constant values, independent of the specific training task or client characteristics. These idealized assumptions fail to reflect the realities of heterogeneous communication networks and heterogeneous computing and communication costs found in practical settings.

To address these realities, this paper proposes a framework that handles heterogeneous communication costs and heterogeneous communication/computational delays. The primary contribution is a generalized asynchronous FL formulation that relaxes cost assumptions regarding both communication channels and clients, while also accounting for the lack of guarantees regarding client participation and the variability of observed costs.

We evaluate PSFT across multiple datasets, including multi-task scenarios, comparing it against a conventional fine-tuning baseline and a control group using a model with random initialization rather than pre-training. We demonstrate that, through a sequence of partial differential equation transformations, the RCHE—which is algebraically equivalent to the reducible DCHE—can be resolved directly, thereby circumventing reliance on the approximation inherent in factorizing the RCHE's operator into first-order components. The RCHE serves as a limiting case of the CHE obtained by setting one parameter to infinity; consequently, its four solution pairs collapse into two, each comprising one finite and one infinite solution. By imposing an appropriate integrability condition on the CHE and selecting a specific value for the second parameter, we derive closed-form solutions for the RCHE that are valid for all values of this second parameter. Finally, we utilize the RCHE to construct a parameterized, parameter-free, and truncated basis for the space of solutions, a tool that proves essential for numerically calculating the monodromy data of the superheaviness. This approach yields solutions that are valid for the RCHE across the entire parameter space, without requiring additional numerical work, thus avoiding the propagation of monodromy parameters from the CHE to the RCHE. Furthermore, we introduce a procedure to derive non-factorizable solutions for general (in)solvable DCHEs from the known solutions of the (solvable) RCHE, without resorting to the use of computer algebra systems. This methodology is demonstrated for each of the 16 (insolvable) supermonodromy classes, resulting in general formulas for the (real) monodromy data of the corresponding CHEs that are directly applicable to the physical problem of electron-positron pair production in a time-varying electric field. Furthermore, the factors obtained in the (insolvable) supermonodromy cases are shown to possess unique properties that preclude the existence of general solutions expressible in terms of heunite functions, thereby preventing potential inaccuracies that could arise from employing heunite functions beyond their region of convergence. This paper presents initial findings on the global minimization of matrix nuclear norm penalties from a data-driven perspective. We establish sufficient conditions for global minimization when recovering a matrix with a fixed, known rank from partially observed entries. From an optimization standpoint, this approach enables the use of reparametrization techniques that reduce the original non-convex problem to a convex one via an orthogonal reparametrization. In this new formulation, the convex objective is minimized over the Stiefel manifold by enforcing the orthogonality constraint explicitly. Using these insights, we demonstrate how to globally minimize both nuclear norm and convex-faithful penalties in matrix completion and robust principal component analysis. Additionally, we numerically demonstrate that a carefully calibrated convex-faithful penalty can effectively denoise a fixed-rank matrix in the presence of Gaussian noise. Finally, we extend these findings to provide sufficient conditions for global minimization with unknown rank under the matrix nuclear norm penalty for both matrix completion and denoising scenarios. Our results indicate that solving the associated convex-optimization subproblems yields global minimizers for these problems, allowing for application to cases where the true rank is either known or can be identified through data-driven spectral analysis. Furthermore, for matrix completion, we show that the data-driven global minimizer corresponds to the previously studied data-driven low-rank embedding. The paper concludes by reporting experiments that compare the empirical performance of various algorithms utilizing either an orthogonal reparametrization or the ELMo algorithm within the convex framework. Additionally, we observe that enforcing orthogonality in this approach typically acts as a regularizer, facilitating the estimation of a rank lower than or equal to the true rank. Finally, our numerical analysis demonstrates that convex-faithful penalties can achieve significantly higher ranks than traditional nuclear norm penalties. Within this framework, researchers investigate how the topological characteristics of these graphs influence the propagation of information, diseases, and other entities between nodes. A prevalent assumption in the field is that node attributes determine propagation patterns and can thus be utilized to predict node similarity. However, this assumption relies on the propagation process revealing the graph's topology, which is not always true. Our research demonstrates that information spreading through both unweighted single-hop and multi-hop processes can mask the graph's structure, even when node in-degrees are used as node features. Furthermore, these results remain robust within the broad class of multi-hop processes where only source node attributes are considered during propagation. Consequently, our findings have significant implications that extend beyond prediction tasks to the accessibility and interpretability of learned models. We have made these results actionable by demonstrating that graph embedding methods can be enhanced to improve the prediction of node attributes and propagation patterns by explicitly integrating additional topological information. We support our claims with empirical evidence, and we include a summary of our results in the context of a recent ICLR review in this discussion. Furthermore, to ensure reproducibility, we have released our data and implementations on GitHub. Finally, our research highlights the intricate relationship between information spreading and topological characteristics, where the strength of these dependencies varies depending on the specific properties of the graph being spread across. Specifically, our studies indicate that while the impact of node features and node degree distributions diminishes as the influence of local topological features, such as node similarity, increases. This suggests that the impact of node degrees is not universal, and researchers should exercise caution when generalizing these results. In summary, these insights provide valuable context for researchers working on related problems. To facilitate this, our code and data are available on GitHub, and we have prepared a FAQ to address common questions and help others apply these insights to their own work. Additionally, graph embedding is shown to be susceptible to adversarial attacks, where adversaries introduce subtle perturbations in node attributes or edges. While existing literature has established the vulnerability of neural network classifiers, our work extends this by demonstrating that graph embedding neural networks are similarly susceptible to attacks targeting both node attribute prediction and information propagation. This vulnerability underscores the need for greater attention to security when deploying such models in real-world scenarios. To support this, we have released our implementation on GitHub. This research represents a novel application of adversarial attacks to information propagation, offering new avenues for future study. Our findings indicate that AMM execution mechanisms cause value erosion for liquidity providers when token exchange rates are volatile. Consequently, AMMs are only viable when token pairs serve high personal utility for investors or when the prices of the tokens in the pair are highly correlated. While a pricing curve with greater curvature mitigates arbitrage risks, it simultaneously diminishes investor surplus. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that AMMs yield the greatest investor surplus for token pairs characterized by a highly predictable price increase. These insights suggest that more sophisticated execution mechanisms, tailored to specific token pairs, have significant potential to enhance the attractiveness of blockchain-based trading. We conclude that triangular arbitrage and dynamic fee structures based on price changes and volatility, such as those employed by AMMs, should be evaluated as optional components in a broader design of token exchanges. Current literature, by focusing exclusively on AMMs, fails to account for the complex trade-offs between liquidity provider and investor interests inherent in execution mechanisms. As a project under the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab, supported by the Department of Energy's National Quantum Initiative, we are constructing a cryogenic infrastructure designed to achieve millikelvin temperatures within an experimental volume measuring roughly 2 meters in diameter and 1.5 meters in height. This platform is engineered to support a three-dimensional qubit architecture utilizing superconducting radio-frequency (RF) and radio-frequency-solenoid (RFS) qubits. Both qubit types are engineered for operation within the RF cavity's RF field, enabling them to be read and controlled through the same circuit. The RFS qubit incorporates a built-in RF antenna featuring an inductive gap, allowing it to couple directly to the RF field. The following paper outlines the design and fabrication of a four-stage, cryorotatable coaxial cavity resonator intended to host up to sixteen RFS qubits and six superconducting flux qubits. These sensing qubits are optimized to detect the frequencies of neighboring rips on the RFS qubit array. Additionally, the manuscript details measurements of the resonator's unloaded quality factor and its cavity mode field structure. Ultimately, the resulting cryomill platform is projected to accommodate up to 100 qubits, with significant scalability potential. By leveraging the inherent high-Q environment and the native RF coupling of both qubit types, this approach promises superior performance. This research was conducted at the National Quantum Initiative National User Facility, quantum facilities at Fermilab, a member of the DOE Office of Science, and is also supported by the U.S. Army Research Laboratory and the U.S. Army Air Force Institute of Research under the Quantum Services Program.

80% of patients may receive inappropriate antibiotics for uncomplicated urinary tract infections (UTIs), largely due to insufficient guidance on prescribing. Although earlier antimicrobial stewardship initiatives have demonstrated that standardizing treatment can decrease antibiotic use, the methodology behind these changes has remained unclear. The public release of hospital antibiotic prescribing data might facilitate the creation of targeted, data-driven interventions. This study examines the potential of leveraging public datasets to enhance antibiotic prescribing practices for UTIs.

**Methods:** We gathered public datasets detailing antibiotic prescriptions for UTIs in England and identified variations in prescribing preferences across different hospitals. We then investigated whether targeting specific antibiotics could be more effective than targeting individual hospitals.

**Results:** Our analysis revealed significant heterogeneity in prescribing preferences among hospitals in England, with certain institutions showing a strong tendency to prescribe particular antibiotics regardless of the individual physician. When focusing on the most commonly prescribed antibiotics, we found that targeting specific drugs led to similar total prescribing rates within hospitals as hospital-targeting approaches, yet the proportion of inappropriate prescriptions remained lower.

**Conclusions:** These findings suggest that interventions should concentrate on restricting the use of specific antibiotics rather than solely aiming to aggregate prescribing behavior at the hospital level. By combining both strategies, it may be possible to achieve a lower overall rate of inappropriate antibiotic usage for UTIs. Furthermore, the methodology can be readily adapted to other conditions and geographic areas by accessing public antibiotic prescribing data. Additionally, we propose that physicians should receive personalized feedback regarding their own prescribing habits.

While EE diverges as the cutoff approaches infinity for infinite systems, this work identifies a specific subtraction scheme within the CFT OPE that eliminates this divergence, yielding a finite result. Consequently, we introduce a new, cutoff-independent definition of EE in critical many-body systems, encompassing both unique and universally valid components. Notably, this finding has critical implications for the convergence of the von Neumann series expansion of EE into entanglement spectrum coefficients (ETC). Specifically, this formulation provides an OPE-based criterion for ETC convergence, particularly for excited states, while also addressing the previously enigmatic issue of potential divergences in ETC for ground states. Additionally, we derive an upper bound for EE and offer a comprehensive analysis of the convergence of ETC in free fermion ground states. Our approach relies on a hybrid framework combining the Majorana fermion model with CFT, a method we also demonstrate facilitates the efficient calculation of entanglement spectrum eigenvalues (ETEV). Furthermore, this synergy enables the generalization of the Fermi-arc phenomenon from excited CFT states to the many-body excited spectrum of free fermion systems. Finally, we show that the ETEV distribution in the excitation spectrum of one-dimensional free fermion ground states (FFLG) adheres to the Wigner semi-circle distribution, with its width determined by the ETC. In summary, this paper presents a novel formulation of EE specifically for critical many-body systems, with this approach forming the foundation for our future research. Additionally, the findings regarding the divergence in von Neumann EE may prove theorems or criteria useful for analyzing entanglement in other many-body systems, such as those at finite temperatures. To address a utility maximization problem featuring an infinite horizon and an infinite number of goods, we employ a direct approach grounded in envelope conditions and Euler equations. Applying this technique, we demonstrate how to reformulate a demand system that explicitly accounts for consumer habit persistence into one that resembles the standard form of a demand system. Furthermore, we examine three distinct consumer habit persistence mechanisms to illustrate how they influence demand function formulation and what specific characteristics of these forms reflect distinct habit persistence types. We demonstrate that our method is applicable to various functional forms, including those based on CES preferences. Additionally, we investigate the link between direct habits and adjustment costs within general equilibrium frameworks. This research offers a valuable tool for formulating utility functions that correspond to demand functions expressing consumer habit persistence. Additionally, the methodology can be extended to scenarios where utility and demand functions are not differentiable at certain points. Finally, analyzing such models requires solving saddle path-stable differential equations, for which we provide a relevant approximation technique. This technique facilitates the efficient and accurate resolution of saddle path-stable differential equations relevant to dynamical systems modeling open economies with endogenous exchange rates. Finally, we apply this approach to reconstruct a demand function based on characteristics of consumers exhibiting adjustment cost habits and habit persistence.

, there is a growing need to detect and analyze anomalies. However, current research is limited by a lack of comprehensive real-world datasets. Existing collections are either too small for thorough evaluation or too heterogeneous in anomaly types to serve as complete benchmarks. Furthermore, prior studies have primarily relied on unsupervised methods, even though many cities have invested resources in labeling real-world datasets. This paper introduces Awari, a large-scale anomaly detection dataset gathered from over 100 smart meters in an entire city within about one year. Awari includes three distinct readings—electricity demand, active power delivery, and frequent switching events—collected continuously for each meter. Additionally, this study evaluates both supervised and unsupervised anomaly detection techniques on Awari. The findings indicate that supervised learning models perform well in identifying meter-level anomalies, such as faulty meters and uncharacteristic consumer behavior. Conversely, detecting spatially correlated city-wide anomalies (e.g., extreme weather events) remains difficult, even with access to ground truth labels. The paper concludes by discussing how these results inform the design of effective anomaly detection systems for smart city infrastructure. Our approach is exact and utilizes the generating functionals of classical Toeplitz and Hankel matrices. Applying this to the time-dependent Hartree-Fock method for electron propagation following X-ray ionization, we address key conceptual issues regarding the formulation of time-dependent mean-field theories. This enhanced convergence enables more accurate prediction of experimental X-ray photoemission spectra with fewer iterations of the time-dependent Hartree-Fock algorithm. Additionally, our findings offer insights into the numerical behavior of mean-field methods in time-dependent scenarios, potentially advancing the algorithm for cases where the mean-field approximation is less accurate. Within the category $Set$, the optimal preorder approximation corresponds to the coequalization of $f$ with a specific morphism that collapses all pairs mapping to the same target element. To establish this result, it is beneficial to employ the category $ \mathbb E ^\wedge$, which consists of sup-lattices defined on sup-preserving maps from bounded sup-lattices in $\mathbb E$. This auxiliary category provides a regular framework for analyzing sup-preserving morphisms and equivalences. This paper extends the classical theory of supertopological spaces, which relies on sup-lattices and sup-preserving maps, to broader contexts involving finitary sup-algebras and sup-lattice morphisms over any regular category $\mathbb E$. The study emphasizes the necessity of data screening to eliminate outliers and the critical role of distribution transformation in capturing the dependence structure of extremes. A power law is observed for the tails of the marginal distributions following the transformation, indicating that both variables share an identical shape parameter of approximately 0.3. By employing copula methods, researchers estimate that for every 10 years, about 3 to 4 hours of simultaneous extremes are expected, compared to roughly 20 to 30 hours involving individual variable extremes. These findings highlight that extreme environmental conditions occur more frequently than previously thought, suggesting that overlooking the correlation between wind and wave fields may lead to a substantial underestimation of severe conditions. This conclusion suggests that design parameters for offshore structures should be derived from the analysis of joint extremes rather than individual variables. Furthermore, the results suggest that relying solely on meteorological oceanographic measurements is insufficient for characterizing joint extreme conditions, as the shorter record lengths typically associated with such data may introduce a similar overestimation of joint extremes. This conclusion is based on analysis of a single measurement, indicating a need for additional research using larger datasets. These findings also support the design criteria recommended by the Joint Committee for North Atlantic Wave and Wind Data. These elements include the frequent occurrence of significant joint extremes, the non-additive nature of extreme events, and the presence of frequent, short-duration excursions into joint extreme zones. These insights facilitate the creation of North Atlantic joint extreme maps for both hourly and six-hourly wave and wind extremes. The resulting maps show that the incidence of joint extremes is significantly higher than when considering only wind or wave extremes separately. The map indicates a rate of approximately 10 days per year for joint extremes and reveals that the North Atlantic's joint extreme conditions are stronger than those in other global regions. However, these datasets often suffer from impractical collection methods and biased distributions, which can negatively influence CLIP's transfer capabilities. To enhance the robustness of the pre-training stage and further boost the efficient transfer performance of the resulting models, this paper introduces an improved CLIP pre-training strategy tailored for practical applications. Specifically, we suggest replacing the open-world image-text contrastive learning paradigm with a close-world multiple choice prediction (MCP) task for text during the image-text pairwise contrastive learning process of CLIP. This MCP task mitigates the negative impact of noisy labels by leveraging the exclusive relationship between images and captions within the training data. Additionally, we incorporate an image-text similarity prediction task into the standard CLIP pre-training objective, allowing for the extraction of high-quality semantic features from image-text pairs while substantially reducing the computational costs during the pre-training phase. Empirical results across 18 widely used downstream tasks validate the effectiveness of our proposed methods. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/zhaojiansheng/Practical_CLIP.
