Although prior research has employed psycholinguistic tools to investigate how transformers handle negation, no study has specifically targeted the negation categories examined in developmental psychology. This work assesses transformer proficiency with these specific categories by formulating the challenge as a natural language inference (NLI) task. We compiled diagnostic questions featuring post-modified phrases and denials as premises, paired with contrasting labels (e.g., "True/False" or "Entailment/Contradiction"). Using the curated dataset ProdiGNC, we found that models like BERT and the CLRP family performed poorly, often treating all such sentences identically. To our knowledge, this represents the first BERT/CLRP fine-tuning study on Post-modification and Denial NLI. Consequently, we demonstrate that CLRP distance-based fine-tuning significantly improves performance on NLI tasks containing post-modifications and denials, establishing a strong baseline for future research. Furthermore, we offer a theoretical explanation for transformer failures in this context by applying Negation Categorization Theory (NCT) to a novel sentence encoding framework, EGS. Under NCT, we show that simply appending the word "not" does not constitute a logical denial, contrasting with cases where "not P" clearly functions as a denial of P. This insight offers a fresh perspective on negation representation within transformers. We hope this research inspires future efforts to develop transformers capable of effectively processing complex negations. Additionally, we anticipate that ProdiGNC could prove valuable for evaluating the EGS model on NLI tasks where BERT struggles. Finally, we recommend further psychological studies examining how BERT and CLRP representations encode different negation categories. Overall, we contend that this first-principles approach to negation categorization within transformers merits additional investigation. However, recent observations indicate that data from the Fermi-LAT satellite deviate from predictions at photon energies exceeding 3 GeV. This study investigates whether an intergalactic magnetic field (IGMF) can resolve this discrepancy by altering the propagation of cosmic ray protons through magnetic curvature. By comparing the predicted DGRB spectra with observational data, we determine that for the intensity of the DGRB to remain below current experimental limits, the average IMF curvature radius must exceed approximately 10 Mpc for IGM proton energies between 10 and 100 Mpc. Furthermore, under these conditions, the average IMF curvature radius approaches the diffusive length scale, causing the mean free path of protons in the IGM to become determined by the size of magnetic curvature regions. This implies a transition in the energy range where the DGRB intensity begins to rise due to the superposition effect. Our findings are consistent with recent research suggesting that the DGRB's observed intensity sets an upper limit on the average IGM magnetic field strength. Additionally, the energy range where our model predicts a shift in the mean free path of IGM protons aligns with recent proposals suggesting the possible existence of a "knee" in the cosmic ray spectrum. Finally, the model's mean free path of IGM protons also agrees with recent estimates of the volume-averaged IGM density derived from quasar absorption spectra. Overall, these results suggest that the intensity of the DGRB can be effectively constrained without requiring an energy cutoff for cosmic ray protons in the IGM. Through a quantitative analysis of key properties using the Hubbard model within mean-field approximation, we determine the optimal filling range for copper oxides. Our findings indicate that cuprates are best described as a mixture of antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic states. This outcome arises because the antiferromagnetic order drives superconductivity, whereas long-range singlet Ferromagnetic order induces a transition to a ferromagnetic state when charge carrier density exceeds a critical threshold. We attribute this behavior to the presence of spin-flip and non-spin-flavoured super-exchange interactions within the mean-field framework. By incorporating electron-electron correlations via the self-energy in a one-loop perturbation, we re-examine the low-temperature phase diagram of cuprates and confirm the emergence of mixed antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic orders. Comparing our results with experimental data reveals that the proposed mechanism can explain the coexistence of antiferromagnetism, ferromagnetism, and stripe order observed in cuprates. Consequently, we propose that the Hubbard model provides a more accurate foundation for understanding the theoretical underpinnings of the emergence of antiferromagnetism, ferromagnetism, and stripe order in cuprates. Finally, we examine the implications of this work for other transition metal oxides. We conclude that the transition between antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, and striped states is not merely a theoretical construct but also holds relevance for understanding the origin of superconductivity in cuprates. This study may also offer new insights into the search for room-temperature superconductors. In the concluding section, we explicitly explore the novel aspects of this research and discuss its novel implications. We hope this novel perspective will inspire further investigations and facilitate the discovery of room-temperature superconductors in the future. However, this conclusion relies on specific assumptions regarding the relative strengths of rotation and turbulence. This study examines three regimes of rotating, turbulent convection: the classical, anomalous, and over-driven. We utilize a fully three-dimensional, global MHD code to simulate these scenarios, as well as a reduced code based on the Boussinesq approximation, to investigate how convection and rotation interact with rotation-dependent dynamamos and magnetic field transport. By comparing magnetic energy spectra and decay times, we observe that the classical dynamo consistently produces more small-scale magnetic energy than the anomalous dynamo, an outcome that is more pronounced during the saturation phase, particularly when magnetic transport is included. These results align with the ideal dynamo simulations we performed, thereby refuting the assumption of anomalous magnetic diffusion. We propose that this discrepancy arises because both the classical and anomalous dynamos exhibit similar large-scale characteristics, including spiral structures and helicity signs, which ultimately drive comparable characteristics in the small-scale magnetic field. These findings offer novel insights into how rotation and turbulence govern small-scale magnetic fields and indicate that rotation and helicity should be treated as independent parameters, which appears to apply to both solar and stellar dynamos. We also demonstrate that magnetic transport significantly impacts the saturated state in all three regimes, primarily by altering the characteristic scales of the small-scale field and its energy cascade. Finally, we highlight that both dynamo models generate characteristic scales consistent with observed convective cores in the Sun and stars, though further, more realistic three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations are required to fully elucidate the specific mechanisms involved. These results hold relevance for both solar and stellar magnetic fields. 2D (or axisymmetric) simulations remain a valuable, computationally efficient tool for analyzing fundamental convective and dynamical processes, yet they fail to accurately represent small-scale and intermediate-scale phenomena in the Sun and stars. The proposed simulation strategy—employing a global model to address fundamental issues and a reduced model to investigate specific scenarios—offers a promising pathway for advancing our understanding of both observed and theoretically significant parameters in various astrophysical contexts. This region features multiple circumstellar disks and binary and triple star systems. We detected the molecular outflow via the $^{12}\mathrm{CO}(J=2-1)$ and $^{13}\mathrm{CO}(J=2-1)$ lines along a north-south axis, with an outflowing gas mass of $\sim 0.03\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$. Analysis of the outflow's position relative to the 1.1 mm continuum peak and the spatial arrangement of young stars suggests the outflow originates from a specific star-forming area. The stellar mass within this area is $\sim 0.1\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$, which aligns with the outflow's position and indicates it likely stems from an individual star or a small group of stars. We propose a novel method to distinguish whether such outflows arise from single stars or binaries. By comparing the area ratio of high-velocity contours to the 1.1 mm continuum size against the velocity area ratio derived from the $^{13}\mathrm{CO}(J=2-1)$ line, we find velocity ratios $\leq 1$ for single-star outflows and $\geq 1$ for those driven by binaries or triples. Applying this criterion to LkCa 44 confirms its molecular outflow is associated with a binary or triple system. This methodology enables the identification of outflow sources and determination of their associated stellar components.

the Standard & Poor 500 index fund. This relative wealth is calculated by dividing the absolute portfolio wealth by the wealth generated if the benchmark were held instead. A primary goal for managers is surpassing this benchmark to deliver the extra returns sought by investors.

A widely used tool for analyzing absolute and relative performance is the performance attribution model, which decomposes differences between manager and benchmark returns into various factors, such as asset class allocation and security selection. Standard attribution models typically evaluate overall performance at the portfolio level, breaking down the total relative return into component effects like asset class selection and allocation.

However, investors may also desire to understand the impact of individual security selections, such as choosing specific stocks over others. To capture this effect, attribution analysis must decompose the total relative return into three components: security selection, security allocation, and interaction between the two. This paper introduces a straightforward and efficient attribution model designed for portfolio selection and allocation analysis that incorporates interaction effects. The model utilizes weighted average decomposition and emphasizes the interaction between selected securities.

The primary contribution of this model is demonstrating that ignoring interaction effects between selected securities can distort attribution results. When interaction effects are accounted for, the total relative return is redefined as the sum of the interaction term alongside the contributions from security selection and allocation. This research validates the model using historical data from the Microsoft portfolio. Additionally, the study provides theoretical proofs to highlight the necessity of including interaction effects in portfolio attribution analysis. Finally, the cross-validation method is applied to verify that the proposed model avoids overfitting the in-sample data. This methodology can be extended to other portfolio selection and allocation studies. By integrating interaction effects, the model enhances the accuracy of attribution analysis while maintaining a simple structure. Ultimately, this improvement offers portfolio managers and investors greater insight into the specific sources of a manager's ability to outperform benchmarks. This work was published in the International Journal of Financial Studies. Keywords: Attribution Analysis; Interaction; Portfolio Selection; Portfolio Allocation. JEL Codes: C38, G11. Page 1 of 20.

While CR networks utilize various multiple access schemes to mitigate inter-CR interference and enhance spectral efficiency, non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) is particularly advantageous in multi-user CR systems. By implementing superposition coding and employing successive interference cancellation (SIC), both strong and weak users can be supported. Furthermore, maximum ratio transmission (MRT) combined with maximum likelihood (ML) detection at the receiver offers a straightforward method to simultaneously improve spectrum efficiency and user throughput. This paper proposes a unified superposition coding scheme that incorporates multiple antennas at the cognitive transmitter, alongside a comprehensive outage analysis for near and far primary users, as well as for weak and strong secondary users. The proposed scheme is evaluated under OFDMA and vector coding frameworks, assuming that all cognitive users are equipped with $M$ antennas, while solving joint power allocation and user pairing optimization problems to maximize overall system throughput. Numerical simulations conducted to demonstrate the proposed scheme's efficacy confirm its effectiveness and efficiency. Additionally, the impact of power splitting and the number of cognitive antennas on overall system throughput is analyzed. Numerical findings indicate that when multiple cognitive users are present, supporting strong users is more beneficial than supporting weak users. Furthermore, increasing the number of antennas at the cognitive transmitter enhances overall system throughput, although it is not an absolute necessity. Finally, joint optimization of power allocation and user pairing is confirmed to be the most effective approach for achieving higher CR network throughput. Overall, the proposed scheme achieves superior throughput performance with minimal complexity. Numerical results also confirm that the orthogonal multiple access (OMA) scheme achieves maximum reliability. All conclusions are backed by corresponding proofs. Finally, the paper confirms the impossibility of achieving higher reliability using power combining (PC) and beam combining (BC) techniques. Addressing the growing issue of data poisoning attacks in machine learning models, researchers have introduced the Data Sanitization (DS) task to identify and remove poisoned samples, allowing robust models to train effectively on cleaned datasets. However, existing DS approaches are constrained to detecting only label-flipping attacks, limiting their practical utility. This paper introduces a new Data Sanitization task called Anomaly Sanitization (AS), which aims to detect diverse data poisoning attacks rather than just label flipping. To solve AS, we develop the Generalized Sanitization Network (GSN), which can be integrated into standard training pipelines without altering the original model architecture. GSN employs a two-stream network: one stream reconstructs the global distribution to identify normal data, while the other reconstructs the local distribution to refine this detection. This design ensures that GSN can effectively handle various AS tasks, including but not limited to label flipping. Extensive experiments on multiple AS scenarios confirm that GSN can successfully identify all different types of data poisoning attacks. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/ChenpengZhang/AS.

Induced Backgrounds (BIB) caused by in-flight muon decays along the beamline, which can hinder the reconstruction of collision products in both hemispheres. These collisions typically involve a signal muon traveling nearly the speed of light and a non-muon recoil target remnant at near-rest. This remnant generates a dense spray of secondaries that suffer severe displacement from the interaction point due to the large impact parameters. The objective is to quantify and characterize these BIB effects on the secondaries associated with this non-muon recoil in order to assess their potential impact on collider physics physics beyond the Higgs factory. Current BIB studies rely on event generators that lack recoil data at large impact parameters. Consequently, this work presents a method to produce such BIB samples using PYTHIA 8 by employing the 4-body decay of a simulated, slightly off-shell muon into a remilion on PYTHIA's color singlet channel, which successfully replicates the observed BIB distributions in simulated events. Furthermore, these event samples are utilized to evaluate the impact of BIB on the B+K and $p\bar{p}$ physics beyond the Higgs factory. The +K channels are investigated using 46 GeV colliders, while b physics is studied with 10 GeV colliders. These studies consider scenarios where no attempt is made to mitigate BIB, ensuring a conservative analysis of potential effects. Additionally, a first look at emulsion calorimeter data from the LHCb BIB measurement experiment is included. This preprint presents a selection of emulsion calorimeter events from LHCb using $\mu^+\rightarrow\mu^-$ decays at $x/c=0.9955\pm 0.0001$ to search for BIB in the pre-scintillator calorimeter. Events with tracks in the 4-momentum measurement detector were selected to investigate potential BIB impacts. No BIB was observed, and all events were consistent with multiple muon $\to$ electron conversions within the detector material. These emulsion calorimeter events are now stored at CERN-RDC for potential future studies. Finally, this work outlines a strategy for the Belle II BIB measurement experiment aimed at the $\mu^+$ factory by proposing a method to enhance the efficiency of muon $\to$ electron searches using the $\mu^-$ decay channel. This approach employs a complex selection criterion that leverages the distinct BIB topology to significantly reduce the background from muon $\to$ electron conversions without introducing additional BIB. fundamental to many emergent quantum phenomena. A notable example is the quantum Hall effect, where two-dimensional electrons in strong magnetic fields display many-body induced localizations. This study examines how this phenomenon, or similar behaviors, manifest in three-dimensional systems. In three dimensions, a disordered electron gas without interactions typically remains delocalized except at zero temperature and zero flux. Many-body interactions shift the critical magnetic field for the localized transition into the finite-temperature region. We present a scaling analysis of the scaling form for the transition field. Furthermore, initial numerical results at zero temperature indicate that for disordered two-dimensional systems, the scaling form is better described by a power law with an infinite width parameter. These findings may assist in clarifying the nature of the localized state observed in ultracold atom simulations. Additional numerical work is currently in progress. We also explore the physical interpretation of the width parameter in the context of many-body renormalization group theory, noting its relevance to other physical scenarios. Based on this interpretation, a universal scaling form is derived for the transition field. Finally, we address the physical meaning of the dynamical scaling exponent, which shifts from 2.0 to 2.3 as the temperature varies. The approach is also applicable to the many-body assisted delocalization of bosons. Our scaling analysis suggests that in the disordered Bose gas, the width exponent is not 6 but a smaller value. This aligns with the observation that exact numerical results for bosons converge more rapidly than those for fermions. We provide a physical justification for this behavior using the many-body renormalization group. Based on this justification, we estimate the universal scaling form of the transition density. Additionally, we demonstrate that many-body interactions can shift the critical interaction strength for Mott insulation from zero to a finite value, a result supported by the many-body renormalization group analysis. Based on the universal scaling form for the Mott transition, we also estimate the critical exponent of the phase transition at zero disorder. Overall, we argue that the many-body renormalization group method is a valuable and effective tool for understanding the body-fixed problem. of forward and inverse initial boundary value problems for equations involving a fractional derivative in time, designed to model diffusion processes. In these models, the diffusion coefficient depends on the solution, meaning it varies with space and time. We demonstrate that the forward problem admits a unique weak solution belonging to specific fractional Sobolev spaces, which are naturally aligned with the definition of the fractional derivative. Furthermore, we prove that the forward operator is continuously invertible within an appropriate set of functions, confirming the well-posedness of the direct problem. This finding is achieved through an appropriate smallness condition on the difference of diffusion coefficients, paired with an appropriate integral metric in the function space. Finally, we provide numerical examples to illustrate the theoretical results, demonstrating that significant errors can arise in both the solution and its norm when attempting to invert the forward operator under conditions where the smallness condition for the diffusion coefficients is not met. These examples highlight the necessity of verifying the smallness condition for the diffusion coefficient, as well as establishing appropriate ill-posedness results and their implications for data errors in solving the inverse problem. Additionally, these examples underscore the importance of employing regularization methods to ensure a stable solution to the inverse problem. This approach is crucial when the forward operator is not surjective and the inverse problem is ill-posed, as a small perturbation in noisy data can lead to a completely different solution. This sensitivity is exacerbated when the forward operator is not invertible, as it lacks an adjoint operator, which is essential for solving the inverse problem, as proven in this study. These examples also validate the conclusions reached in earlier research by the authors regarding invertibility and the absence of an adjoint operator for nonsmooth coefficients. Specifically, when the diffusion coefficients are not sufficiently smooth, the forward operator is compact, yet its invertibility cannot be guaranteed without additional conditions. This issue is particularly evident when the forward operator is compact, as a small perturbation in noisy solution data can significantly impact the solution to the inverse problem. The examples also reinforce the conclusions drawn in this work concerning data errors and their effect on solving the inverse problem, as well as validate findings from previous research by the authors. These findings are consistent with those from other studies on similar inverse problems. However, accurately extracting heartbeats from signals is challenging, especially when dealing with noisy data. This paper introduces a method to estimate IBI by utilizing a generative model to approximate a key property of IBIs: their generation as a sum of two independent stochastic processes. These processes can be characterized using a functional principal component analysis and a time series analysis. Specifically, we estimate the underlying functions and parameter coefficients via a projected stochastic estimation, then use a Poisson cluster process to simulate the IBIs. This approach enables the reconstruction of target IBIs, even from highly corrupted signals. Consequently, we propose a detection strategy that estimates instantaneous IBIs by fitting the observation to the simulated IBIs. Evaluation on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrates that this proposed approach achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods. Notably, when IBIs are simulated, our method outperforms existing techniques. On real-world datasets, the best-performing algorithm yields results similar to those of the proposed model. Ultimately, this study highlights the significance of considering the intrinsic properties of IBIs for effective heart rate monitoring. To address this, we propose estimating dynamic spillover effects within network structures. Specifically, we estimate an intervention effect on the direct target and on other units who receive the intervention indirectly through their position in the network. Under the assumption of linear partial equilibrium effects and sparse, exogenous inter-unit connections, the network spillover effect arises from unit-to-unit spillovers multiplied by the network leverage. Leverage is determined by in-degrees, which depend on how intervention allocation varies along the network's transmission paths. Applying this framework to a randomized beauty contest experiment, we find that contestants directly instructed to take higher risks induce others to do the same via indirect transmission paths. We characterize the magnitude and significance of these network spillover effects for any given unit. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this methodology applies to any experiment featuring a partial or full randomized intervention allocation and a network of physical or social units with interacting interests and decision-making processes. This analysis offers crucial insights into the viability and interpretation of experiments aiming to study decision-making and interest interactions between and within units. The accompanying R package, `netEval`, facilitates these analyses. We illustrate the framework using two examples: a computer science experiment from 2018 regarding how programmers collaborate and influence each other in code, and an economic study from 2019 on how policy-makers interact to achieve shared goals. While Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs) have proven effective for identifying feasible solutions, the variety and complexity of real-world issues make it challenging to encode them into a standard CSP framework. To overcome this, this paper introduces a novel framework capable of handling rich CSPs. It utilizes a representation called the Constraint Knowledge Graph (CKG), which models problem characteristics through nodes representing variables, domains, and constraints, rather than defining the problem via a specific set of constraints. For instance, finding an optimal travel route between multiple cities by minimizing travel time can be modeled as a CSP using a CKG. Furthermore, rather than treating the CSP kernel as a traditional CSP, this study models it as a Satisfiability Problem (SAT). Consequently, determining the optimal solution for a specific problem reduces to formulating a corresponding SAT instance and resolving it. Additionally, we can determine whether a problem satisfies all constraints and optimize variable values within their domains. The proposed CKG-SAT successfully modeled 11 practical CSP cases, including resource allocation, scheduling, and travel route planning. For many of these, the method yielded satisfactory results, while also providing a definitive answer when a problem was found to be infeasible.

To address CKG-SAT involving node sets larger than current SAT solvers can handle, this paper proposes a new SAT solver, MN2SAT. MN2SAT employs a two-step approach for large CKG-SAT problems: first, it partitions the CKG into smaller subgraphs based on node density; second, it determines the solution by calculating the satisfiability of these subgraphs and applying a two-stage search algorithm. Experimental results demonstrate that MN2SAT solves CKG-SAT problems up to 10,000 nodes—approximately 100 times larger than those solvable by conventional SAT solvers—within practical computation times. Thus, the proposed CKG and the newly developed MN2SAT offer a promising framework for solving large-scale CSPs. Finally, the source code for both the CKG construction method and MN2SAT is made publicly available. The source code for both the CKG construction and MN2SAT can be accessed at https://github.com/edamLab/ckgsat. The paper's source code is accessible at https://github.com/edamLab/ckgsat. 1. **Phase 1**: For graphs where vertex degrees do not exceed $\Delta$, we perform multiple iterations to progressively reduce $\Delta$. Each iteration begins by identifying all vertices with an odd degree, matching them in pairs, and then matching remaining unmatched vertices (including those with odd degrees) in groups of three. After these matches are established, edges within each group are connected to form paths, ensuring that the maximum degree within every path does not exceed $\Delta/2$.
2. **Phase 2**: All paths from Phase 1 are sorted, organizing the graph into a collection of disjoint chains.
3. **Phase 3**: Each chain is sorted using an external sorting algorithm, arranging all vertices in order of increasing labels.
4. **Phase 4**: Within the sorted vertex sequence, the second largest label associated with each vertex is determined by scanning through all vertices and their neighbors.

This algorithm completes in $O\bigl(n+m+\Delta(\log\Delta+\log\log\Delta)\bigr)$ time and $O(n+m)$ words of memory. The need to incorporate weight into network measures can significantly enhance our understanding of systems like social networks, biological pathways, and social media networks. Despite this, a comprehensive set of weighted network metrics suitable for analyzing mixed graphs (containing both directed and undirected edges) is lacking. This study presents a collection of mixed-network metrics derived from a weighted generalization of the edge eigencentrality metric. We demonstrate that eigenvalues and eigenvectors provide an intuitive method for identifying structurally influential nodes based on their position within the network. Numerical simulations indicate that these metrics effectively distinguish between more and less structurally important nodes and edges. a prominent method for integrating prior physical knowledge into learning frameworks. This paper examines the application of PINNs to a specific domain: stochastic systems where only a limited number of observations from the stationary probability density function (SPDF) are available. We identify scenarios where PINNs fail to converge and propose a novel strategy to ensure convergence. As a representative case, we analyze a stochastic differential equation (SDE) describing a particle with friction and mass moving in one dimension under the influence of multiplicative noise. Under these conditions, PINNs attempt to learn the SPDF subject to sparse dataset constraints while adhering to the Fokker-Planck equation (FPDE) as prior knowledge. Our proposed solution involves appending a regularization term to the loss function; this approach enables the recovery of the true SPDF using PINNs without requiring extensive training, even with minimal FPDE prior knowledge and sparse datasets. In this context, the PINN functions more effectively as a parametric model for the SPDF, with conventional regularization techniques playing a critical role in integrating FPDE prior knowledge meaningfully. Furthermore, we explore additional examples and offer insights into broader implications. We also present a comparative analysis of various PINN methodologies for SPDF learning, demonstrating that a Poisson equation-based model outperforms others. Finally, we address the influence of certain study assumptions, noting that relaxing the small-mass assumption in SDEs without modifying the learning framework leads to PINN convergence failure. These findings highlight the necessity of regularization when mass is small for accurate PINN-based SPDF learning. Additionally, we discuss the model's ability to generalize when PINNs are applied to data distributions distinct from the training data. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of utilizing an incorrect FPDE as prior knowledge, observing that the PINN still yields highly accurate SPDF estimates. Together, these results underscore the PINN's robustness in learning SPDFs for stochastic systems, even with scarce data and imperfect prior knowledge. Our contributions include a novel learning framework for PINN-based SPDF acquisition, an in-depth analysis of PHYSICS-of-MATH within PINNs, and a rigorous study of data and prior knowledge impacts on the convergence process. This research is particularly relevant for applications in inverse problems, such as parameter identification, for stochastic systems. The source code is available at: https://github.com/zhengruiyang/PINN-for stochastic systems. This bound is derived without assuming large sample sizes and is formulated based on the distance between the critical regions of the initial test for independence and each procedure under consideration. Specifically, we demonstrate that the post-test power is bounded from below by the initial procedure's test size minus twice the product of two Hellinger distances: the first between the null distribution of the first stage and that of the second, and the second between an alternative distribution for the first stage and that of the second. Consequently, we prioritize the uniform integration over all alternative distributions for the first stage when comparing procedure performances. Leveraging this result, we introduce a method combining a test based on exact permutation distribution with a test utilizing a liberal asymptotic critical region, defined as the complement of the union of rejection regions for exact permutation tests. Simulation studies confirm that this new procedure outperforms established methods in finite samples. Finally, we apply the procedure to a widely accessible dataset indicating superior results. Crucially, this scheme avoids the need to select between permutation-based tests and those using asymptotic critical regions, which typically require sample sizes exceeding 50. Finally, it guarantees a non-asymptotic minimum post-test power. These findings represent the first application of triangle inequality-based reasoning to fixed-effects multiple comparison procedures. To our knowledge, this also marks the first demonstration that permutation tests achieve the same asymptotic post-test power as liberal asymptotic-based procedures, a result derived by demonstrating that a test based on exact permutation distribution is equivalent to one using a liberal asymptotic critical region. Furthermore, we illustrate that specific tests utilizing liberal asymptotic critical regions are incompatible with permutation-based approaches. Finally, we demonstrate that permutation methods are not merely asymptotically more powerful but also more sensitive to deviations from model assumptions. Finally, all proofs and derivations are provided in the supplementary materials. All procedures, including those from existing literature, are implemented in an R package, mcptool, which is made publicly available. We include a function to estimate a procedure's post-test power and another to visualize its theoretical performance relative to other methods. Additionally, the package offers a function to conduct the proposed procedure and another to execute exact permutation tests. Using this package, users can easily replicate any simulation study. mcptool requires R version 4.0.0 or higher. However, we show that even minor defects can suppress or produce a transverse electric field within valley bands, making the emergence of a true valley Hall drift current unlikely in practical systems where defects are inescapable. By applying Drude-Boltzmann kinetic theory, we establish a quantitative framework for the VHE, highlighting the critical roles of the drift distance and the ratio between the density of states at the gap and the carrier density. Specifically, in intrinsically clean systems with finite gap, the drift distance must surpass the ratio of mobility to gap to achieve unitary valley Hall conductivity, thereby revealing the VHE in the linear regime where it is independent of electric field strength and mobility. Conversely, in realistic disordered systems, an intrinsic field arises in valley bands due to disorder scattering, which can be interpreted as a finite drift distance. While this allows the VHE to be observed at finite electric fields and mobilities, it also leads to backscattering that diminishes the resulting valley current. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between this intrinsic field driven by disorder and the anomalous Hall effect caused by impurities in ferromagnetic thin films. Through these analyses, we conclude that detecting the VHE and achieving a valley-dependent Hall conductivity exceeding 1/e remain highly challenging tasks.

This vulnerability often stems from biases in training data or the absence of specialized data cleaning processes. While adversarial examples are known to generalize poorly across datasets, their presence can still introduce new biases that affect performance on unseen data. This paper presents an analysis of how the number of adversarial examples and the balance between clean and adversarial data influence the performance of Neural Networks, specifically focusing on the impact of data cleaning methods. Furthermore, it explores how the topology of the training dataset affects the resulting neural network architectures. Experiments were conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets, utilizing both Random Forest and Neural Network models. The use of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to construct topological datasets allowed researchers to observe performance variations based on whether the test data was derived from the same distribution as the training data or a different one. The findings indicate that the presence of noise within the training set—whether generated synthetically or through adversarial examples—significantly alters the performance of both Random Forest and Neural Network models. Furthermore, the study confirms that applying data cleaning techniques enhances both performance and accuracy. Finally, utilizing GanTop datasets for both training and testing yields superior model performance compared to using unstructured or biased data sets. These results were validated across Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs), Clean Datasets, and Adversarial Datasets. The key conclusion is that both the topology of the training data and the application of data cleaning techniques substantially improve model accuracy. This paves the way for future work in automatically selecting and integrating both clean and adversarial examples during the training data generation phase to further optimize neural network models. A graph complementator for H is defined as a hypergraph sharing the vertex set with H but where each vertex's degree matches the size of its nearest edge minus two. A hypergraph H is considered complete if it possesses a graph complementator. The study establishes that for vertex sets with five or more vertices, the only non-free hypergraphs that are complete are those that are both odd and co-odd. Furthermore, it identifies specific families of free hypergraphs—those odd and not odd, even and not co-even, even and co-odd, or neither even nor co-odd—of which the only complete representatives are those featuring the famous famous triangle (V, {V1, V2, V3}). These findings lead to two notable consequences: 2n-dimensional odd-permanent matrices are diagonalizable, and there exists a unique 3x3 symmetric, even, positive, and semidefinite matrix with a determinant of one that is not the identity, which is the Floyd matrix. Additionally, these results imply that every complete hypergraph with a minimum edge size of three contains at least one vertex with a degree of at least three, and the total number of its edges is bounded above by 2n-1 choose 2. Furthermore, the famous famous triangle (V, {V1, V2, V3}) is the unique minimal complete hypergraph for the case where the vertex set size n equals five. The paper also provides necessary and sufficient conditions for a hypergraph to be complete. Finally, it constructs numerous examples of hypergraph complementsators, including those for Pascal's triangle, a Sierpiński-like figure, a triangle of triangles, a tetrahedron-like figure, a Sierpiński-like tetrahedron-like figure, a simple cube-like figure, a cube-like figure with a hole, a cube-like figure with a hole and with Sierpiński-like faces, a complete tetrahedron-like figure, and a complete tetrahedron-like figure with Sierpiński-like faces, all of which are derived from well-known n-dimensional geometric figures. The paper concludes by posing several conjectures and open problems, the resolution of which would significantly advance current research. We introduce a universality concept that unifies the kinetic properties—specifically kinetic wetting and line tension—acquiredduring undercooling across different liquid-to-vapor systems. Constraint-based optimization was employed to reconstruct the breathing command, revealing that respiratory control during this hypoxic experiment relied on two subsets of parameters. The first subset was active during normoxia, while a second subset became active as CO2 rose and O2 fell. This two-stage parameterization enabled the reconstruction of breathing patterns with a correlation coefficient exceeding 0.99 against a high-fidelity respiratory inductance plethysmography signal from the same session. Although Pruning and Quantization are established techniques for reducing model size, directly applying them to encoder-decoder architectures compromises the performance of major transformers. This study examines the well-posedness of systems governed by such equations subject to dynamic boundary conditions. For the heat equation with dynamic boundary conditions, we employ a semigroup generated by an unbounded operator on $L^2$-spaces to demonstrate well-posedness. Under conditions of ultrastrong coupling between electrons and the cavity's electromagnetic field, vacuum fluctuations induce the dynamical stabilization of a quasistationary polariton state trapped at the center of the repulsive potential. When the kinetic energy of an incoming free electron matches the energy of this confined state, an extremely efficient resonant nonelastic scattering process occurs, accompanied by the emission of a cavity photon. We demonstrate that the probability of this resonance can approach 100% even for coupling strengths modestly below the threshold for stable polariton formation. Additionally, we explore the application of this resonance nonelastic scattering phenomenon to electron-based control of the coupled electron-photon system. These findings are anticipated to be relevant for various experimental setups, including those involving free electrons or electron beams within Fabry-Perot cavities, semiconductor quantum wells, or two-dimensional micro- and nanocavities. Furthermore, the proposed method of ultrastrong nonelastic scattering offers a noninvasive means to prepare the coupled electron-photon system far from its ground state, enabling the investigation of strongly correlated quantum many-body states, such as superconducting dome in the Landau-Fermi-liquid to BCS superconductor transition, the density-dependent shift from parity-symmetric to antisymmetric states in pair-box qubits, and the Pauli-exclusion-principle-dependent Pauli spin-blockade of a Cooper pair tunneling through a quantum dot. This preparatory technique for coupled electron-photon quantum states with high photon occupancy opens new avenues for photon-based quantum information processing and spectroscopy. We support these predictions, which await experimental verification, with a detailed theoretical discussion of the nonelastic scattering process, its parameters, and its wide applicability across diverse physical systems. We also examine a related process of resonant elastic scattering facilitated by virtual pair creation and annihilation of a polariton, analyzing its nonelastic scattering limit and its role in depolarization during the noninvasive preparation of the strongly correlated quantum many-body state. This study investigates the feasibility of replacing the torque motor in a 3-DOF biped robot with fully compliant spring actuators. Addressing the inherent instability, we employ a feedback linearization controller designed to stabilize the linearized system and compensate for non-linearities, including those introduced by the spring actuators and external disturbances. Although feedback linealization is a established method, we adapt it for fully compliant robots, specifically accounting for control strategies that extend beyond simple actuation, such as energy harvesting and storage. To mitigate open-loop instability, the controller applies stored spring energy during the swing phase by appropriately modulating the spring stiffness. Simulation results validate the proposed concept and highlight the significant performance improvements achievable with spring-based actuators. A dual gradient flow method is introduced to approximate this solution using noisy data. Given the ill-posed nature of the problem, the flow exhibits semi-convergence, necessitating a carefully selected stopping time to obtain reasonable approximations. We examine various strategies for choosing this stopping time, including {\it a priori} rules, the discrepancy principle, and the heuristic discrepancy principle, all of which ensure that the generated solutions converge to the true solution $A^{-1}(y)$ as the noise level approaches zero. Furthermore, under appropriate assumptions regarding the source condition and the behavior of the regularized solutions relative to data noise, the study establishes meaningful error estimates and convergence rates for the dual gradient flow method. Finally, the theoretical findings are illustrated through numerical experiments. These findings extend and refine certain results presented in~\cite{Hofr}. Additionally, we prove that, under suitable conditions, the results for dual gradient flow methods in noisy settings can be derived directly from those applicable to homogeneous problems. This insight significantly reduces the effort required to extend analogous results to dual source flow methods in noisy environments. Finally, we explore the connection between the discrepancy principle and the control measure problem within dual gradient flow methods. The resolution of this question provides a foundation for deriving the continuity principle in noisy data scenarios. Additionally, it enables the generalization of results from homogeneous discrepancies to noisy discrepancies, as demonstrated in~\cite{CZ19}. Finally, the continuity principle is applied to analyze the parameter choice rule of the discrete control measure in dual gradient flow methods, yielding the following outcomes: (i) The control measure, solved via the parameter of the dual gradient flow method, converges to the solution of the control measure as the time parameter approaches zero. ### I. Introduction

Light-field (LF) cameras, which capture four-dimensional information including two spatial, two view, and intensity dimensions, have emerged as a promising technique for high-quality image reconstruction. By leveraging multi-view information and advanced algorithms, LFs are well-suited for image super-resolution (LR), a task crucial for enhancing image quality and detail preservation. However, existing LFs generally suffer from two primary limitations. First, handling high-frequency content remains a significant challenge for current LFs. Second, existing state-of-the-art methods often rely on complex, computationally intensive alignment algorithms, resulting in high computational costs. Addressing these two challenges is critical for advancing LF image reconstruction. This paper introduces a novel LR method designed to overcome these obstacles. Specifically, we propose a new LR framework that effectively overcomes high-frequency challenges and utilizes simple alignment techniques to integrate multiple views, thereby reducing computational costs.

First, we propose a novel deep LF pyramid method capable of significantly improving LR performance. Second, we introduce a new 3D-CNN cost function that effectively integrates additional views and requires minimal computational resources. Experimental results indicate that our proposed methods significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art approaches. The remaining content of this paper is organized as follows: Section II provides an overview of related work, covering image LR, LF reconstruction, and LR via LF cameras. Section III details the proposed methods. Section IV presents experimental results and discussions. Finally, Section V concludes the study. The proposed system is available at: https://github.com/zhengliang/LF-3D-CNN.

This approach aims to reduce latency and enhance throughput in home environments equipped with multiple WiFi devices and networks. Unlike traditional fixed-parameter configurations, our method re-tunes essential settings in real-time to align with current and predicted operational conditions, thereby optimizing overall WiFi performance. We assessed the solution's efficacy by simulating up to seven overlapping 802.11n networks, each with five stations, and four 802.11ac networks, each with four stations. Simulation results demonstrate that our Q-learning-based strategy significantly outperforms both un tuned and traditionally tuned parameter settings in terms of latency and throughput, even under scenarios involving simultaneous data transfers and fluctuating bandwidth. The proposed algorithm is highly versatile and can be readily extended to support other 802.11, WiGig, and WiFi-related protocols and parameters. Furthermore, to ensure practical feasibility, we conducted comprehensive analysis and comparison of computational requirements and communication overhead on associated devices. Our findings indicate that the method remains viable even when accounting for these factors. Finally, we validated the solution's effectiveness in a real-world experimental setup within a typical home WiFi environment. Both simulation and experimental outcomes confirm that our method achieves superior performance compared to other schemes, while also maintaining lower power consumption and requiring shorter tuning durations. Consequently, this technique is well-suited for deployment in actual next-generation home WiFi networks.
